exam.name: CompTIA CySA+
exam.note: Domains and weights follow the CS0-003 exam objectives. Check comptia.org for the current exam version before booking. Lessons marked AU bonus are not exam content - they cover Australian context you will use on the job.

lessons.title: Architecture concepts for analysts
lessons.summary: You cannot spot abnormal until you know what normal looks like in your environment. CySA+ expects you to understand how logging, segmentation, identity and encryption shape what an analyst can see and defend.
points: Log ingestion: time synchronisation (NTP) is essential - without consistent timestamps you cannot correlate events across systems. Know your log retention and what each source actually records.
OS concepts: Windows Registry, file structure, system processes, hardening baselines. Configuration drift from a hardened baseline is itself an indicator.
Infrastructure: serverless, virtualisation and containers change where logs live and how long assets exist.
Network architecture: on-premises vs cloud vs hybrid, segmentation, Zero Trust (never trust, always verify; verify every request), SASE (network + security delivered from the cloud), SDN.
Identity and access management: MFA, SSO, federation, Privileged Access Management (PAM), Passwordless, Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB).
Encryption: PKI, SSL/TLS inspection. Data loss prevention (DLP) and protecting PII and cardholder data.
lessons.examTip: When a question asks how to correlate events from several devices and the timestamps disagree, the answer is almost always time synchronisation (NTP).
lessons.onTheJob: Write down your org's 'normal': typical login countries, admin hours, standard software. That baseline turns a vague alert into a fast decision.

quiz.q: An analyst cannot build an accurate timeline because firewall and server logs show the same event minutes apart. What should be fixed first?
quiz.explain: Consistent time across sources (NTP) is the prerequisite for correlation and timelines.

quiz.q: Which principle best describes Zero Trust?
options: Trust devices on the internal network
Continuously verify every access request regardless of location
quiz.explain: Zero Trust removes implicit trust based on network location and verifies each request.

quiz.q: A company wants visibility and policy control over employee use of cloud SaaS apps. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explain: A Cloud Access Security Broker sits between users and cloud services to enforce policy and give visibility.

lessons.title: Indicators of malicious activity: network
lessons.summary: Network indicators are patterns in traffic that suggest compromise. The exam gives you a scenario or a log snippet and asks which indicator it shows.
points: Bandwidth consumption: unexpected spikes, especially outbound, can mean exfiltration.
Beaconing: regular, periodic callbacks to the same host (e.g. every 60 seconds with small jitter) - classic command-and-control (C2).
Irregular peer-to-peer communication: workstations talking directly to each other (SMB, RDP) can mean lateral movement.
Rogue devices on the network: unknown MAC addresses, unauthorised access points.
Scans and sweeps: one source touching many ports (port scan) or many hosts (sweep).
Unusual traffic spikes and activity on unexpected ports: e.g. HTTP on a non-standard port, or DNS traffic that is far too large (possible DNS tunnelling).
lessons.examTip: Regular interval + small payload + same destination = beaconing. Large outbound volume to a new destination = exfiltration.
lessons.onTheJob: Long, random-looking subdomains in DNS queries (e.g. a8f3k2...example.com) at high volume are a strong DNS tunnelling signal.

quiz.q: A host connects to the same external IP every 300 seconds, sending about 200 bytes each time. What is this most likely?
quiz.explain: Small, regular, periodic connections to one destination are typical beaconing.

quiz.q: Which observation most strongly suggests lateral movement?
options: A workstation making SMB connections to many other workstations
A spike in inbound web traffic
DNS queries to a known CDN
quiz.explain: Workstation-to-workstation SMB/RDP is unusual peer-to-peer traffic often linked to lateral movement.

quiz.q: An analyst sees a very high volume of DNS queries with long random subdomains to one domain. What should they suspect?
quiz.explain: Encoding data in subdomain labels is the signature of DNS tunnelling.

lessons.title: Indicators of malicious activity: host and application
lessons.summary: Host and application indicators show up on endpoints and in app logs. Many map directly to MITRE ATT&CK persistence and privilege escalation techniques.
points: Host: unexpected processor or memory spikes, drive capacity changes, unauthorised software, malicious processes, unauthorised changes, privilege changes, data exfiltration, abnormal OS process behaviour, file system changes, registry changes, unauthorised scheduled tasks.
Persistence spots to know: Run/RunOnce registry keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folders, WMI subscriptions.
Application: anomalous activity, introduction of new accounts, unexpected output, unexpected outbound communication, service interruption, application logs.
Social engineering and obfuscated links are also listed indicators - think phishing and URL shorteners.
Living off the land: attackers use built-in tools (PowerShell, certutil, rundll32, wmic) so 'legitimate binary doing odd things' is a key pattern.
Parent-child process anomalies, e.g. winword.exe spawning powershell.exe, are high-fidelity detections.
lessons.examTip: A new local admin account or a new scheduled task created at 3am on a server is a host-based persistence indicator.
lessons.onTheJob: In M365 environments, a new inbox rule that moves or deletes emails containing 'invoice' or 'payment' is a top BEC indicator - check for it on every compromised mailbox.

quiz.q: Which process relationship is most suspicious?
quiz.explain: Office applications spawning scripting engines is a classic malicious macro pattern.

quiz.q: An attacker adds a value under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. What are they trying to achieve?
quiz.explain: Run keys execute at logon, giving persistence.

quiz.q: Using certutil.exe to download a payload is an example of what?
quiz.explain: Abusing trusted, built-in binaries is 'living off the land' (LOLBins).

lessons.title: Analyst tools: SIEM, SOAR, EDR and friends
lessons.summary: CySA+ tests whether you know which tool answers which question. Match the tool to the job.
points: SIEM: aggregates and correlates logs, alerts on rules. SOAR: automates response with playbooks and integrations.
EDR: endpoint telemetry, process trees, isolation. XDR extends this across email, identity and cloud.
Packet capture: Wireshark (GUI analysis) and tcpdump (command-line capture). Full packet capture shows payloads; NetFlow shows only metadata (who talked to whom, how much).
DNS and IP reputation: WHOIS, AbuseIPDB. File analysis: VirusTotal, strings, hashing (SHA-256) to identify known samples.
Sandboxing: detonate suspicious files in an isolated environment (e.g. Joe Sandbox, Cuckoo) to observe behaviour.
Common techniques: pattern recognition, interpreting suspicious commands, email analysis, file analysis, user behaviour analysis (UEBA).
lessons.examTip: Need to know exactly what was in a conversation? Packet capture. Need to know who talked to whom over a month cheaply? NetFlow.
lessons.onTheJob: Before uploading a file to a public sandbox or VirusTotal, check that it does not contain company or customer data - uploads can be visible to others. Search by hash first.

quiz.q: Which tool automates response steps such as disabling an account and opening a ticket when an alert fires?
quiz.explain: SOAR orchestrates and automates response playbooks across tools.

quiz.q: An analyst needs to see the actual payload of an HTTP request. Which data source is required?
quiz.explain: Only full packet capture contains payload contents.

quiz.q: Why should an analyst search VirusTotal by hash before uploading a suspicious document?
options: Hash lookups return more detailed sandbox results
Uploading may expose sensitive content to third parties
Hash search also cleans the file
quiz.explain: Uploaded files can be shared with researchers and vendors; hash lookups reveal nothing new.

lessons.title: Email analysis: headers, SPF, DKIM, DMARC
lessons.summary: Email is the number one initial access vector, and in real estate it is the front line of payment redirection fraud. Know how to read headers and the three email authentication standards.
points: SPF: a DNS TXT record listing which servers may send mail for a domain. Checks the envelope sender (Return-Path).
DKIM: a cryptographic signature added by the sending server; the receiver verifies it with a public key published in DNS. Proves the message was not altered and came from the domain's infrastructure.
DMARC: tells receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail AND requires alignment with the visible From domain. Policies: p=none (monitor), p=quarantine, p=reject. Also provides reporting.
Headers: read Received lines bottom-up to trace the path. Compare From, Reply-To and Return-Path - a mismatched Reply-To is a classic BEC trick.
Look-alike domains: examp1e.com vs example.com style typosquats, extra hyphens, different TLDs. Display-name spoofing shows a trusted name with an unrelated address.
Embedded links: hover/decode to see the true destination; watch for URL shorteners and QR codes (quishing).
lessons.examTip: SPF = who may send. DKIM = message integrity and signing domain. DMARC = policy + alignment + reporting. DMARC needs SPF or DKIM to pass AND align.
lessons.onTheJob: For a payment-change request, the authentication results can all pass if the sender's real mailbox was compromised. Verification must be out-of-band: call a known number from your records, never a number in the email.

quiz.q: Which record tells receiving mail servers to reject messages that fail authentication checks?
quiz.explain: DMARC publishes the policy (none/quarantine/reject) applied when checks fail.

quiz.q: When tracing an email's path, how should Received headers be read?
quiz.explain: Each server prepends a Received header, so the oldest hop is at the bottom.

quiz.q: A vendor email passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC but asks to change bank details. What is the best next step?
options: Reply to the email to confirm
Call the vendor on a number already on file
Forward it to the vendor's other address
quiz.explain: A genuinely compromised mailbox passes all checks; verify out-of-band using known contact details.

lessons.title: Threat intelligence and threat hunting
lessons.summary: Threat intel turns raw data about adversaries into decisions. Threat hunting is the proactive search for threats that existing alerts missed.
points: Threat actor types: APT/nation-state, organised crime, hacktivists, insider threats (intentional and unintentional), script kiddies, supply chain.
Intel types: strategic (big picture, for leaders), operational (campaigns, TTPs), tactical (IoCs like IPs and hashes).
Collection sources: open source (OSINT, social media, blogs, CERTs like ACSC), closed source (paid feeds, ISACs, information sharing communities).
Intel quality: timeliness, relevance, accuracy, and confidence levels.
Sharing standards: STIX (the language/format for describing threat intel) and TAXII (the transport protocol for exchanging it).
Threat hunting: start with a hypothesis (e.g. 'an attacker is using stolen session tokens'), focus on likely targets, use IoCs and IoAs, active defence such as honeypots.
lessons.examTip: STIX = what (structure). TAXII = how (transport). IoC = evidence something happened. IoA = behaviour showing an attack in progress.
lessons.onTheJob: Subscribe to ACSC partnership alerts if your org is eligible - Australian-specific intel is usually more relevant than global feeds.

quiz.q: Which standard is used to transport threat intelligence between organisations?
quiz.explain: TAXII is the transport protocol; STIX is the data format.

quiz.q: A hunt begins with 'Attackers may be abusing OAuth app consent in our tenant.' This is an example of what?
quiz.explain: Threat hunting is hypothesis-driven.

quiz.q: A board briefing about which threat actors target the property sector is which type of intelligence?
quiz.explain: High-level, decision-making intel for leadership is strategic.

lessons.title: Frameworks: ATT&CK, Kill Chain, Diamond Model
lessons.summary: Frameworks give you a shared vocabulary to describe attacks, find gaps in detection and communicate clearly.
points: MITRE ATT&CK: a knowledge base of adversary tactics (the why - e.g. Persistence) and techniques (the how - e.g. T1053 Scheduled Task). Used to map detections and find coverage gaps.
Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command & Control, Actions on Objectives. Break any link to stop the attack.
Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis: every event has four core features - Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim - plus meta-features. Good for pivoting between related events.
Unified Kill Chain: combines Kill Chain and ATT&CK into a fuller attack lifecycle.
OSSTMM (Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual) and OWASP Testing Guide: methodologies for security testing.
Australian context: the ASD Essential Eight maturity model is the local baseline most auditors ask about.
lessons.examTip: Diamond Model = four corners (Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim). Kill Chain = seven ordered stages. ATT&CK = matrix of tactics and techniques.
lessons.onTheJob: Tag your incident tickets with ATT&CK technique IDs. After a few months you will see which techniques hit you most and where detections are thin.

quiz.q: Which model analyses intrusions using adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim?
quiz.explain: Those are the four core features of the Diamond Model.

quiz.q: In the Cyber Kill Chain, which stage comes immediately after Delivery?
quiz.explain: Recon, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, C2, Actions on Objectives.

quiz.q: In MITRE ATT&CK, 'Credential Access' is an example of a:
quiz.explain: Tactics are the adversary's goals (columns); techniques are how they achieve them.

lessons.title: Process improvement and automation
lessons.summary: A good SOC reduces repetitive work so analysts spend time on judgement. CySA+ covers automation, standardisation and basic scripting literacy.
points: Standardise processes: playbooks and runbooks make response consistent and measurable.
Automate where it is safe: enrichment (IP reputation, user lookup), ticket creation, low-risk containment. Keep a human in the loop for high-impact actions.
Team coordination and single pane of glass: fewer consoles, shared context.
Scripting literacy: read basic Python, PowerShell and Bash; understand JSON and XML data formats and regular expressions for parsing logs.
APIs and webhooks connect tools; SOAR uses them to orchestrate.
Efficiency also means tuning: reducing false positives improves detection by reducing alert fatigue.
lessons.examTip: If a question describes analysts doing the same enrichment steps on every alert, the answer is automation/SOAR, not hiring more analysts.
lessons.onTheJob: Learn enough KQL (Kusto) to query Defender and Sentinel - it is the fastest skill upgrade for an M365 shop.

quiz.q: Which regex matches an IPv4-looking string most simply?
quiz.explain: Four groups of digits separated by literal dots. (It does not validate 0-255, but finds candidates.)

quiz.q: What is the best reason to keep a human approval step before automatically disabling an executive's account?
options: The business impact of a false positive is high
quiz.explain: High-impact actions need human judgement to avoid costly false-positive disruption.

quiz.q: Which data format uses key-value pairs in braces and is common in API responses?
quiz.explain: JSON is the standard API format.

lessons.title: Tooling: triaging an EDR detection
lessons.summary: EDR tools raise detections from endpoint behaviour, not just file signatures. Good triage answers three questions quickly: is it malicious, how far has it gone, and should the host be isolated now or watched a little longer.
points: Start with the process tree: parent, child and the full command line. An Office app or email client (winword.exe, excel.exe, outlook.exe) spawning powershell.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe or rundll32.exe is a high-fidelity sign of a malicious document.
Compare parent/child pairs with normal: services.exe starting svchost.exe is expected. svchost.exe started by explorer.exe, or running from outside C:\Windows\System32, is not.

Read the command line: encoded PowerShell (-enc / -EncodedCommand), hidden windows (-w hidden), download cradles (IEX with a web download) and LOLBins fetching files (certutil -urlcache) are classic signs.

Hash and reputation: check the file's SHA-256 against threat intel and against your own fleet (how many hosts have it?). A signed, widespread binary lowers concern. A rare, unsigned file in AppData or Temp raises it. Unknown reputation is not the same as clean.

Scope: search every endpoint for the same hash, command line, domain or IP. Check what the process did next: network connections, files written and persistence created (Run keys, scheduled tasks, services).

Isolate vs monitor: isolation stops spread and C2 but alerts the attacker and stops the user working. Isolate at once for ransomware behaviour, credential dumping or lateral movement. Monitor only briefly, when risk is low and scope is needed, and record who made the call.

EDR network isolation normally keeps the host connected to the EDR console, so you can still collect memory and files after isolating it. Reimaging before collecting evidence destroys what you need to scope the incident.
lessons.examTip: When a scenario shows an Office application spawning a scripting engine or LOLBin, think malicious macro or document. The best next step is usually to isolate the host and collect evidence, not to reimage straight away.
lessons.onTheJob: Write a short triage note on every EDR detection: the process tree, your verdict, the evidence for it and the action taken. Repeated false positives then become tuning requests instead of noise.

quiz.q: An EDR detection shows excel.exe as the parent of powershell.exe running with -EncodedCommand. The user says they just opened an invoice attachment. What is the best next step?
options: Isolate the host and collect evidence before further analysis
Close it as a false positive because Excel is a signed Microsoft binary
Reimage the laptop immediately without investigating
Wait for a second detection before taking any action
quiz.explain: Office spawning encoded PowerShell right after an attachment is opened is a high-fidelity sign of a malicious macro. Isolation limits spread and C2 while preserving evidence; reimaging first destroys the evidence needed to scope the incident.

quiz.q: A detection flags an unsigned executable in a user's AppData folder. Its SHA-256 hash returns no threat intel results and appears on no other endpoint. What is the best interpretation?
options: Unknown reputation is not proof of safety, so analyse its behaviour and treat it as suspicious
The file is clean because no threat intel source has flagged it
The file is definitely malware because every unsigned file is malicious
The hash is probably wrong because every file has a known reputation
quiz.explain: New or custom malware often has no reputation yet. A rare, unsigned binary in a user-writable folder warrants behavioural analysis (process activity, sandbox) rather than a quick close. Plenty of legitimate software is unsigned, so unsigned alone does not prove malice.

quiz.q: An EDR shows a process reading LSASS memory on a file server, followed by new SMB connections from that server to several workstations. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Keep monitoring for a week to learn the attacker's objectives
Uninstall the EDR agent to stop the alerts
Run a vulnerability scan against the server
quiz.explain: Credential dumping followed by lateral movement is an active compromise. The risk of further spread outweighs the value of watching longer, so contain now and collect evidence through the EDR console.

lessons.title: Tooling: secure email gateway workflows
lessons.summary: A secure email gateway (SEG) filters mail for spam, phishing, malware and spoofing, and holds suspicious messages in quarantine. Analysts spend much of their day deciding what to release, what to purge and what user-reported phish tells them.
points: Filtering layers: sender IP and domain reputation, authentication results (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), content and URL analysis, attachment sandboxing, and policy rules such as blocking executable attachments.

Quarantine review: check why the message was held (the verdict and the rule that fired), the true sender domain and Return-Path, the authentication results, and every link and attachment before deciding.

Releasing safely: detonate attachments in a sandbox, check where links really go, confirm the sender out of band if in doubt, release only to the original recipients and record why. A user saying they are expecting it is not enough.

Header analysis: read Authentication-Results for the spf, dkim and dmarc verdicts and the Received lines bottom-up for the path. DMARC passes only if SPF or DKIM passes for a domain that aligns with the visible From domain.
User-reported phish: triage the report, then search for every copy of the message (sender, subject, URL or attachment hash) and remove it from all mailboxes, not just the reporter's.
Close the loop: block the sender, domain or URL at the gateway, check click logs (URL rewriting or proxy) to find anyone who interacted, and thank the reporter. Feedback keeps people reporting.

False positives cost money too: a real contract stuck in quarantine harms the business. Tune with narrow rules, never by allow-listing an entire free-mail domain or a whole sender domain that has failed authentication.
lessons.examTip: After confirming one reported email is malicious, the best answer usually searches for and removes every copy across the organisation, then blocks the indicators. Containment is organisation-wide, not one mailbox.
lessons.onTheJob: In real estate, quarantined 'contract', 'deposit' and 'bank details' emails are high-risk and high-pressure. Release them only after verifying the sender on a known phone number, never one taken from the email itself.

quiz.q: A user asks for a quarantined email to be released because they are expecting a document from a new client. The attachment is a password-protected ZIP and the sender's domain was registered last week. What should the analyst do?
options: Keep it quarantined and verify the sender through a known contact method before any release
Release it because the user is expecting it
Release it and ask the user to scan the ZIP with antivirus first
Forward the ZIP to the user's personal email so the corporate network stays safe
quiz.explain: Password-protected archives stop the gateway inspecting the contents, and newly registered domains are a classic phishing sign. A user's expectation is exactly what attackers exploit, so verify out of band first.

quiz.q: A quarantined message shows: spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.example.net; dkim=pass header.d=example.net; dmarc=fail header.from=example.com. Why did DMARC fail?
options: Neither the SPF nor the DKIM domain aligns with the From domain example.com
SPF failed for the sending server
The DKIM signature did not verify
The message had no Return-Path header
quiz.explain: SPF and DKIM both passed, but for example.net. DMARC needs at least one passing result whose domain aligns with the visible From domain. A spoofer can easily pass SPF and DKIM for a domain they own.

quiz.q: Three users report the same phishing email and the analyst confirms it is malicious. What is the most effective next step?
options: Search all mailboxes for the message, remove every copy, then block the sender and URL
Delete the message from the three reporters' mailboxes only
Forward the phishing email to all staff so they can recognise it
Reset the passwords of the three users who reported it
quiz.explain: Reporters are usually a fraction of the recipients. Purging all copies and blocking the indicators contains the campaign; click logs then show who interacted and needs follow-up. The reporters did the right thing and have no reason for a reset unless they entered credentials.

lessons.title: Asset discovery and vulnerability scanning
lessons.summary: You cannot protect what you do not know about. Vulnerability management starts with accurate asset inventory, then scanning designed around the environment.
points: Asset discovery: map scanning, device fingerprinting, CMDB. Unknown assets are often the vulnerable ones.
Credentialed vs non-credentialed: credentialed scans log in and see patch levels and configuration (more accurate, fewer false positives). Non-credentialed shows the attacker's outside view.
Agent-based vs agentless: agents suit laptops that leave the network; agentless needs network reach.
Internal vs external scans; active vs passive (passive listens to traffic, no load on targets).
Special considerations: scan scheduling, operations impact, sensitivity levels, segmentation, regulatory requirements (e.g. PCI DSS needs quarterly external ASV scans).
OT/ICS and fragile legacy systems: use passive monitoring or careful, low-intensity scans.
lessons.examTip: Fewer false positives and accurate patch levels = credentialed scan. Testing what an outside attacker sees = external non-credentialed scan.
lessons.onTheJob: Distributed offices often have forgotten devices (old NAS boxes, printers, routers). Cross-check scan results against your asset list and chase every unknown.

quiz.q: Which scan type gives the most accurate view of missing patches on Windows servers?
quiz.explain: Credentialed scans can read installed software and patch levels directly.

quiz.q: Laptops are rarely on the corporate network. Which approach ensures they are still assessed?
quiz.explain: Agents report in from wherever the device is.

quiz.q: A fragile legacy control system crashes when actively scanned. What is the best alternative?
quiz.explain: Passive monitoring identifies software and versions from traffic without touching the device.

lessons.title: Reading scan output and CVSS
lessons.summary: Scanners produce noise. The analyst's job is to validate findings and prioritise by real risk, not just by score.
points: CVSS v3.1 base metrics: Attack Vector (Network, Adjacent, Local, Physical), Attack Complexity (Low/High), Privileges Required (None/Low/High), User Interaction (None/Required), Scope (Unchanged/Changed), Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability impact (None/Low/High).
Severity bands: 0.1-3.9 Low, 4.0-6.9 Medium, 7.0-8.9 High, 9.0-10.0 Critical.
Validate: true positive, false positive (reported but not there), true negative, false negative (there but missed - the dangerous one).
Prioritise with context: exploitability (is it in CISA KEV? is there a public exploit? EPSS score), asset value, exposure to the internet, compensating controls.
Tools: Nmap (discovery, ports, versions), Nessus / OpenVAS / Qualys (vuln scanners), Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP (web proxies), Nikto (web server scanner), Arachni.
Cloud: Scout Suite, Prowler, Pacu for cloud configuration assessment. Debuggers and multipurpose tools like Metasploit appear too.
lessons.examTip: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N = remotely exploitable, easy, no privileges, no user interaction - the worst combination. Prioritise these on internet-facing systems.
lessons.onTheJob: Use the CISA KEV items in the News tab: if a scanner finding matches a KEV entry, it jumps the queue regardless of CVSS.

quiz.q: Which CVSS metric value makes a vulnerability exploitable remotely over the internet?
quiz.explain: Attack Vector: Network means exploitable remotely.

quiz.q: Which result is most dangerous for an organisation?
quiz.explain: A false negative is a real vulnerability the scanner missed, so nobody fixes it.

quiz.q: A CVSS 6.5 vulnerability is in CISA KEV and on an internet-facing VPN. A CVSS 9.1 issue is on an isolated test server. Which first?
quiz.explain: Known exploitation plus internet exposure outweighs a raw base score.

lessons.title: Common vulnerability types
lessons.summary: You need to recognise vulnerability classes from a snippet of log, URL or code and know the core fix for each.
points: Injection: SQL injection (' OR 1=1 --), command injection, LDAP injection. Fix: parameterised queries, input validation.
Cross-site scripting (XSS): reflected, stored, DOM-based. Fix: output encoding, Content Security Policy.
CSRF: tricks a logged-in user's browser into making a request. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.
SSRF: makes the server fetch a URL the attacker chooses - often internal metadata services (169.254.169.254 in cloud).

Directory/path traversal (../../etc/passwd), local and remote file inclusion. Buffer overflows, race conditions, insecure deserialisation, broken access control (IDOR), security misconfiguration, use of components with known vulnerabilities, cryptographic failures.
OWASP Top 10 is the standard web reference; broken access control is #1 in the 2021 list.
lessons.examTip: <script> in a URL parameter = XSS. ' OR 1=1 = SQL injection. ../ sequences = traversal. 169.254.169.254 = SSRF against cloud metadata.
lessons.onTheJob: Most real-world breaches use boring classes - misconfiguration, known vulnerable components, and broken access control - more than exotic exploits.

quiz.q: A web log shows GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd. What is being attempted?
quiz.explain: ../ sequences attempt to escape the intended directory.

quiz.q: Which control best prevents SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Parameterised queries separate code from data.

quiz.q: Changing /account?id=1001 to id=1002 shows another customer's data. What is this?
options: Insecure direct object reference / broken access control
quiz.explain: The server fails to check the user is authorised for that object (IDOR).

lessons.title: Controls, mitigation and risk
lessons.summary: Not everything can be patched immediately. CySA+ tests control types, compensating controls and the risk management responses.
points: Control categories: managerial (policies, risk assessments), operational (people-run: training, guards), technical (firewalls, encryption).
Control functions: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, responsive.
Compensating control: an alternative that reduces risk when the primary control is not possible (e.g. isolate an unpatchable system on its own VLAN).
Risk responses: accept, transfer (insurance, contracts), avoid (stop the activity), mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact).
Patching and configuration management: testing, maintenance windows, exceptions with expiry dates and owner sign-off.
Inhibitors to remediation: MOUs, SLAs, organisational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality, legacy and proprietary systems.
lessons.examTip: Cyber insurance = transfer. Retiring a risky service = avoid. Signing off a known risk = accept. Patching = mitigate.
lessons.onTheJob: Every risk acceptance should have an owner, a reason and a review date. Untracked 'temporary' exceptions are how old vulnerabilities survive for years.

quiz.q: A legacy app server cannot be patched, so it is moved to an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs. This is a:
quiz.explain: An alternative control that reduces risk when the primary fix is unavailable.

quiz.q: Buying cyber insurance is which risk response?
quiz.explain: Insurance transfers financial impact to a third party.

quiz.q: Security awareness training is categorised as which control type?
quiz.explain: It is implemented by people rather than technology, so operational.

lessons.title: Attack surface, SDLC and threat modelling
lessons.summary: Reducing attack surface and building security into software development prevents vulnerabilities rather than chasing them later.
points: Attack surface management: edge discovery, passive discovery, security controls testing, penetration testing and adversary emulation, bug bounties, attack surface reduction.
Secure SDLC: requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance - security at every stage ('shift left').
Testing: SAST (static, source code), DAST (dynamic, running app), IAST (instrumented), fuzzing, SCA (software composition analysis for third-party libraries).
Threat modelling: identify assets, threats, and mitigations at design time. STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Secure coding: input validation, output encoding, session management, authentication, data protection, parameterised queries.
Supply chain: SBOMs (software bill of materials) show what components a product contains.
lessons.examTip: SAST = source code, no execution. DAST = running app, black-box. SCA = third-party libraries and their CVEs.
lessons.onTheJob: Your external attack surface includes SaaS tenants and marketing sites built by agencies. Many breaches start on a forgotten subdomain.

quiz.q: Which testing approach analyses source code without executing it?
quiz.explain: Static Application Security Testing reads code at rest.

quiz.q: In STRIDE, what does the R stand for?
quiz.explain: Repudiation: denying an action occurred, addressed with logging and non-repudiation.

quiz.q: Which tool type identifies known vulnerable open-source libraries in an application?
quiz.explain: Software Composition Analysis checks dependencies against vulnerability databases.

lessons.title: AU bonus: the Essential Eight
lessons.summary: ASD's Essential Eight is the baseline Australian organisations are measured against. It is not CySA+ exam content, but you will be asked about it at work constantly.
points: 1. Patch applications - especially internet-facing ones, fast (within 48 hours when an exploit exists, at higher maturity).
2. Patch operating systems - same idea for OS and firmware; replace unsupported versions.
3. Multi-factor authentication - phishing-resistant MFA is expected at higher maturity levels.
4. Restrict administrative privileges - least privilege, separate admin accounts, no admin browsing or email.
5. Application control - only approved executables, scripts and installers can run.
6. Restrict Microsoft Office macros. 7. User application hardening (e.g. block ads/Java in browsers, disable risky features). 8. Regular backups - tested, and protected from modification or deletion.
Maturity levels 0-3: ML1 resists commodity attacks, ML2 moderately skilled targeted attacks, ML3 skilled adversaries. Aim for the same level across all eight.
lessons.examTip: Not on CySA+, but maps neatly to exam ideas: application control is preventive, backups are corrective, and patching is mitigation.
lessons.onTheJob: Learn which maturity level your organisation is targeting and where the gaps are - it frames almost every improvement conversation with management.

quiz.q: Which Essential Eight strategy prevents unapproved executables from running?
quiz.explain: Application control allow-lists approved code.

quiz.q: Essential Eight Maturity Level 1 is designed to resist which adversaries?
options: No adversary - it is documentation only
quiz.explain: ML1 targets widely available tools and opportunistic attacks.

quiz.q: What makes backups effective against ransomware under the Essential Eight?
options: Storing them on the same file server
Protecting them from modification/deletion and testing restores
Encrypting them with the same admin account
quiz.explain: Backups must survive the attacker and be proven restorable.

lessons.title: Tooling: reading a vulnerability scan report
lessons.summary: A scan report is a list of claims, not a to-do list. The analyst's job is to validate findings, weed out false positives and rank what is left by real risk: severity, exploitability and the importance of the asset.
points: A finding usually shows the check name, CVE IDs, CVSS score and vector, affected host and port, evidence (what the scanner actually saw) and suggested remediation. Read the evidence: it tells you how much to trust the finding.

Severity is not priority. CVSS describes how bad a flaw is in general. Exploitability (CISA KEV listing, public exploit code, EPSS probability) and asset criticality (internet-facing, sensitive data, business critical) decide what is fixed first.

Common false positives: version-banner checks on systems where the vendor backported the fix without changing the version string, and software that is installed but disabled or unreachable. Validate before raising a ticket.

Credentialed vs non-credentialed: a credentialed scan logs in and reads installed patches and configuration, so it finds more (including local and client-side issues) with fewer false positives. A non-credentialed scan shows the outside view but has to guess more.

False negatives hide in gaps: hosts that were offline, firewalled from the scanner, failed authentication or were left out of scope. Check the coverage and authentication-success summary, not just the findings list.
Group by fix, not by count: one missing cumulative update can produce dozens of findings, and installing it closes them all.
Rescan after remediation to verify the fix, and track recurrence. A finding that keeps coming back points to a golden image or configuration management problem.
lessons.examTip: When two findings have similar CVSS scores, the exam usually wants the one that is internet-facing, actively exploited (in KEV) or on the most critical asset fixed first.
lessons.onTheJob: Before sending results to system owners, sort by exploitability and asset criticality, remove validated false positives with a note explaining why, and group findings under the single fix that closes them. Owners act on short, accurate lists.

quiz.q: A non-credentialed scan reports a critical OpenSSH vulnerability on a Linux server based on its version banner. The owner shows that the distribution's security update, which backported the fix, is installed. What is this finding most likely?
quiz.explain: Distributions often backport security fixes without changing the upstream version number, so banner-based checks report a flaw that is already fixed. A credentialed check of the installed package confirms it.

quiz.q: Which finding should be remediated first?
options: CVSS 8.1 on an internet-facing VPN appliance, listed in CISA KEV
CVSS 9.8 on an isolated lab server with no path to production and no known exploit
CVSS 7.5 on an internal print server with no known exploit
CVSS 5.3 information disclosure on the public website
quiz.explain: Confirmed exploitation in the wild (KEV) plus internet exposure on a critical access point outweighs a higher base score on an isolated system nobody is exploiting.

quiz.q: A team switches from non-credentialed to credentialed scans and the number of findings rises sharply. What is the most likely reason?
options: Logging in lets the scanner see installed software, patch levels and local configuration that are invisible from the network
Credentialed scans generate far more false positives
The scan credentials gave attackers access to the hosts
Non-credentialed scans only test web applications
quiz.explain: With credentials the scanner can read patch levels and local software (browsers, PDF readers, runtimes), revealing real issues a network-only scan cannot see. Credentialed scans usually reduce false positives, not increase them.

lessons.title: The incident response lifecycle
lessons.summary: CySA+ follows the NIST SP 800-61 style lifecycle. Know the phases, their order, and what belongs in each.
points: Preparation: IR plan, playbooks, tools, training, tabletop exercises, contact lists, legal and comms arrangements.
Detection and analysis: identify, validate and scope the incident; determine severity and impact.
Containment, eradication and recovery: stop spread, remove the threat, restore and validate systems.
Post-incident activity: lessons learned, root cause analysis, evidence retention, update plans and controls.
The process is a cycle: lessons learned feed back into preparation.
Attack methodology frameworks (Kill Chain, ATT&CK, Diamond) help you scope and describe what happened.
lessons.examTip: If a question asks when to hold a lessons-learned meeting: post-incident. When to build playbooks and run tabletops: preparation.
lessons.onTheJob: Know who to call before you need them: IT lead, legal, privacy officer, insurer's breach hotline, and how to reach ACSC (1300 CYBER1).

quiz.q: Running a tabletop exercise belongs to which phase?
quiz.explain: Exercises prepare the team before real incidents.

quiz.q: What should happen with lessons-learned outputs?
options: Fed back into preparation (plans, controls, training)
quiz.explain: IR is a cycle; improvements feed preparation.

quiz.q: Determining how many hosts are affected and the incident's severity happens in:
quiz.explain: Scoping and severity are part of analysis.

lessons.title: Detection, analysis and evidence handling
lessons.summary: Good analysis is built on good evidence. Collect it in the right order, preserve it properly and document everything.
points: Order of volatility (most to least volatile): CPU registers/cache, RAM and running processes, network state, temporary files, disk, remote logs, archival/backup media.
Chain of custody: who collected the evidence, when, how it was stored and every transfer - required for legal use.
Integrity: hash evidence images (SHA-256) at collection and verify later. Use write blockers for disks.
Legal hold: preserve relevant data once litigation is reasonably anticipated.
Data and log analysis: build a timeline, scope with IoCs, check for related accounts and hosts.
Severity and impact: consider data sensitivity, number of systems, recoverability, business criticality.
lessons.examTip: Always capture memory before powering off a system - shutting down destroys RAM evidence (running processes, network connections, keys).
lessons.onTheJob: For cloud and M365 incidents your 'disk image' is often the unified audit log and sign-in logs. Export them early - retention limits can delete evidence.

quiz.q: Which should be collected first from a live compromised host?
quiz.explain: RAM is far more volatile than disk.

quiz.q: What proves evidence has not been altered since collection?
options: Storing it on a USB stick
quiz.explain: Matching hashes demonstrate integrity; chain of custody documents handling.

quiz.q: Legal counsel expects a lawsuit about an incident. What should be issued?
quiz.explain: A legal hold preserves potentially relevant data.

lessons.title: Containment, eradication and recovery
lessons.summary: Containment buys time, eradication removes the attacker, and recovery restores normal operations safely.
points: Containment: isolation (EDR isolate, pull from network), segmentation, blocking IoCs, disabling accounts, revoking sessions/tokens.
Balance: containing too early can tip off an attacker; too late lets them spread. Consider monitoring for scope first when safe.
Eradication: remove malware and persistence, reimage rather than 'clean', reset credentials (including service accounts and krbtgt twice for domain compromise).
Recovery: restore from known-good backups, patch the root cause, monitor closely for re-infection.
Sanitisation of media: clear, purge, destroy. Validate restored systems before returning to production.
Compensating controls and scope reduction can apply while a full fix is in progress.
lessons.examTip: Reimaging is more reliable than cleaning. For account compromise, resetting the password is not enough - also revoke sessions and remove attacker-added MFA methods and rules.
lessons.onTheJob: M365 account compromise checklist: reset password, revoke sessions, review MFA methods, remove malicious inbox rules and forwarding, check OAuth app consents, review sent items, notify likely recipients.

quiz.q: After resetting a compromised user's password, the attacker still has access. What was most likely missed?
quiz.explain: Existing session tokens can remain valid until revoked.

quiz.q: Why is reimaging preferred over cleaning malware from a host?
options: It keeps the attacker's tools available for analysis
It removes hidden persistence you might miss
quiz.explain: You cannot be sure cleaning found everything; reimaging returns a known-good state.

quiz.q: Isolating an infected laptop from the network is which step?
quiz.explain: Isolation limits spread - containment.

lessons.title: AU bonus: BEC and payment redirection playbook
lessons.summary: Payment redirection fraud is one of the biggest cyber risks for Australian real estate: attackers impersonate agents, vendors or conveyancers to divert deposits, rent or settlement funds. Speed matters - banks can sometimes recall funds if alerted quickly.
points: How it works: compromise or spoof a mailbox, watch conversations, then send 'updated bank details' at the moment money is about to move.
Immediate actions: contact the sending bank's fraud team at once to attempt a recall, report via ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au), and preserve the emails with full headers.
Mailbox triage: sign-in logs (odd locations, impossible travel, legacy auth), new inbox rules, forwarding to external addresses, OAuth app consents, sent items and deleted items.
Scope: who else received messages from the compromised account? Warn them quickly.

Prevention: out-of-band verification of all bank detail changes using known numbers, phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, external email tagging, DMARC at p=reject, and staff training on settlement-time scams.
Privacy: a compromised mailbox often contains personal information - assess against the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (see 4.2).
lessons.examTip: Maps to CySA+ Domain 3: containment = revoke sessions and remove rules; eradication = remove attacker MFA/OAuth apps; recovery = monitor the mailbox; post-incident = training and verification process changes.
lessons.onTheJob: Write a one-page 'bank detail change' procedure for agents and property managers. The best control here is a phone call, not a product.

quiz.q: A client has just transferred a deposit to fraudulent bank details. What is the most time-critical action?
options: Contact the bank's fraud team to attempt a recall
quiz.explain: Fund recovery chances drop sharply with time.

quiz.q: Which mailbox artefact most commonly reveals a BEC attacker hiding replies?
options: Inbox rules moving or deleting messages
quiz.explain: Attackers create rules to hide replies and warnings from the real user.

quiz.q: Which control best stops payment redirection even if a mailbox is compromised?
options: Out-of-band verification of bank detail changes
quiz.explain: A call to a known number defeats the attacker regardless of email compromise.

lessons.title: Preparation and post-incident activity
lessons.summary: The work before and after an incident decides how bad the next one is.
points: Preparation: incident response plan, playbooks per scenario (ransomware, BEC, data breach), tools, training, documentation, contact lists.
Tabletop exercises: talk-through scenarios with stakeholders to test the plan without touching systems.
Business continuity (BC) and disaster recovery (DR): RTO (how fast must it be restored) and RPO (how much data loss is tolerable).
Post-incident: forensic analysis, root cause analysis, lessons learned, updating the plan and controls.
Root cause analysis looks for the underlying failure (e.g. no MFA on legacy auth), not just the immediate trigger.
Retention: keep incident evidence and records according to legal and policy requirements.
lessons.examTip: RTO = time to restore. RPO = acceptable data loss window (drives backup frequency).
lessons.onTheJob: Run a 30-minute BEC tabletop with a branch manager and finance. It finds process gaps faster than any audit.

quiz.q: Backups run every 4 hours. What does this most directly support?
quiz.explain: Backup frequency determines maximum data loss: RPO.

quiz.q: A discussion-based walk-through of a ransomware scenario with executives is a:
quiz.explain: Tabletop exercises are discussion-based.

quiz.q: Root cause analysis primarily aims to:
options: Identify the underlying failure so it does not recur
quiz.explain: RCA targets the underlying cause to prevent recurrence.

lessons.title: Vulnerability reporting and metrics
lessons.summary: Vulnerability management only works if the right people see the right information and act on it. Metrics show whether it is working.
points: Reports should include: vulnerabilities found, affected hosts, risk score, mitigation, recurrence, prioritisation.
Compliance reports vs action plans: one shows status for auditors, the other drives remediation (configuration management, patching, compensating controls, awareness, changing business requirements).
Inhibitors to remediation: MOUs, SLAs, organisational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality, legacy systems, proprietary systems.
Metrics and KPIs: trends, top 10 lists, critical vulnerabilities and zero-days, SLO/SLA compliance.
Stakeholder identification and communication: tailor detail to the audience - executives want risk and trend, admins want hosts and fixes.
Track mean time to remediate by severity and how many findings exceed their SLA.
lessons.examTip: If remediation is blocked because a vendor contract forbids changes to an appliance, the inhibitor is an SLA/MOU or proprietary system - expect a compensating control as the answer.
lessons.onTheJob: Executives respond to trends: 'critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days dropped from 42 to 9 this quarter' beats a 200-page scan export.

quiz.q: A vendor-managed system cannot be patched without voiding support. This is an inhibitor caused by:
quiz.explain: Vendor-controlled proprietary systems often restrict changes.

quiz.q: Which audience needs host-level remediation detail?
quiz.explain: Admins need specific hosts and fixes; executives need risk summaries.

quiz.q: What does tracking 'percentage of critical findings fixed within SLA' measure?
quiz.explain: It measures how well remediation meets agreed timelines.

lessons.title: Incident reporting and communication
lessons.summary: During an incident, communication can do as much damage or good as the technical response. Know who needs to hear what, and what the law requires in Australia.
points: Stakeholders: legal, executives, HR (insider cases), public relations, customers, regulators, law enforcement. Use pre-approved comms channels; assume email may be compromised.
Incident report contents: executive summary, who/what/when/where/why, recommendations, timeline, impact, scope, evidence.
Metrics: mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), mean time to remediate, alert volume.
Root cause and lessons learned feed the final report.

AU: Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (Privacy Act) - if an eligible data breach is likely to result in serious harm, notify the OAIC and affected individuals as soon as practicable; a suspected breach must be assessed within 30 days.
AU: under the Cyber Security Act 2024, businesses with annual turnover above $3 million must report ransomware or extortion payments to ASD within 72 hours.
lessons.examTip: The executive summary goes first and is written for non-technical readers: what happened, impact, what is being done, what decisions are needed.
lessons.onTheJob: Never speculate about attribution or data loss to customers or media - route statements through legal and comms. Facts, actions, next update time.

quiz.q: Which metric measures how long it takes on average to notice an incident?
quiz.explain: Mean Time To Detect.

quiz.q: Who should approve external statements during a breach?
quiz.explain: External communication has legal and reputational consequences.

quiz.q: Under Australia's NDB scheme, how long does an organisation have to assess a suspected eligible data breach?
quiz.explain: A reasonable and expeditious assessment within 30 days; notify as soon as practicable once confirmed.

lessons.title: Security metrics and KPIs
lessons.summary: Metrics turn SOC and vulnerability work into evidence leaders can act on. Know what each one measures, where its clock starts and stops, and how it can mislead.
points: Mean time to detect (MTTD): average time from when an incident starts (or first malicious activity) to when it is detected.

Mean time to respond (MTTR): average time from detection to the start of response or containment. Mean time to remediate is longer: detection (or discovery of a vulnerability) until the fix is complete.
Dwell time: how long an attacker was present before detection, usually measured from initial compromise to detection. Lower MTTD drives lower dwell time.
Alert volume on its own says little. Pair it with the true positive rate: rising alerts with flat confirmed incidents means tuning is needed, not more staff.
Vulnerability KPIs: percentage of findings fixed within SLA by severity, vulnerability age, open criticals over time, recurrence of previously fixed findings.
Averages hide outliers. One server open for 400 days can wreck a mean; report the median too and list the exceptions separately.
A KPI measures performance against a target (e.g. 95% of criticals patched within 14 days). A metric is just a measurement. Trends over time beat single snapshots.
lessons.examTip: Detect = how long until we noticed. Respond = how long from noticing to acting. Remediate = how long until it is actually fixed. Read where the question's clock starts and stops.
lessons.onTheJob: Pick a handful of metrics and report them the same way every month: MTTD, MTTR, criticals past SLA, and phishing reports. Consistent definitions matter more than clever dashboards.

quiz.q: Logs show an attacker first accessed a mailbox on 1 March. The SOC detected the activity on 21 March and contained it on 22 March. What was the dwell time?
options: It cannot be measured until eradication is complete
quiz.explain: Dwell time runs from initial compromise to detection: 1 to 21 March is 20 days. The 1 day from detection to containment is response time.

quiz.q: Over three months, SIEM alert volume has tripled while the number of confirmed incidents has stayed flat. What is the best next step?
options: Tune or retire noisy detection rules to cut false positives
Hire more analysts to keep up with the alert queue
Report the higher alert volume to executives as improved detection
Disable correlation rules and rely on EDR alerts only
quiz.explain: More alerts without more true positives means a falling true positive rate. Tuning reduces alert fatigue; reporting volume as success is misleading.

quiz.q: An executive asks whether the SOC has become faster at acting on incidents once they are spotted. Which metric answers this most directly?
quiz.explain: MTTR starts at detection. MTTD and dwell time measure how long it took to notice, not how fast the team acted afterwards.

lessons.title: Stakeholder communication and escalation
lessons.summary: The same incident needs a different message for the board, the sysadmins, legal and the regulator. Escalating at the right time, through the right channel, is part of the response.
points: Escalation follows the incident response plan: a severity matrix and criteria (data involved, systems affected, spread) decide who is told and how quickly. Re-assess severity as facts change.
Executives and the board: business impact, current risk, what is being done, cost and the decisions needed from them. No raw technical detail.
Technical teams: indicators, affected hosts and accounts, exact actions and deadlines.
Legal: involve early. They advise on notification obligations, evidence preservation, legal hold and keeping advice privileged. Regulator notifications are usually made through or with legal.
HR is involved in insider cases; PR/communications handles customers and media; law enforcement involvement is a decision made with legal and management.
Use out-of-band channels (phone, pre-arranged secure chat) when email or chat may be compromised, and share on a need-to-know basis so a suspect or attacker is not tipped off.
Set an update cadence: state facts, actions and the time of the next update. Separate confirmed facts from assumptions and never speculate about attribution or data loss.
lessons.examTip: When a question asks what to tell executives, choose impact, risk and decisions needed. When it asks how to communicate while systems may be compromised, choose an out-of-band channel.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a printed or offline contact list for the IR team, legal, insurer and key managers. If the mail tenant is compromised, that list is how the response starts.

quiz.q: An analyst finds evidence that an attacker has full access to the organisation's email tenant. How should the analyst notify the incident response team?
options: By phone or a pre-arranged out-of-band channel
By email to the IT distribution list
By posting in the company-wide chat channel
By raising a normal-priority helpdesk ticket
quiz.explain: If email is compromised, the attacker may read the notification. Out-of-band communication keeps the response hidden from them.

quiz.q: An alert first triaged as a low-severity phishing report is now confirmed as an account compromise with access to customer records. What should happen next?
options: Reclassify the severity and escalate according to the IR plan's escalation criteria
Keep the original severity so the ticket metrics stay consistent
Wait for the weekly security report to inform management
Email all affected customers immediately before scoping is complete
quiz.explain: Severity is re-assessed as facts change, and escalation criteria (such as personal data being involved) trigger notification of the right people. Customer notification follows scoping and legal advice.

quiz.q: The analyst is preparing a ten-minute briefing for the board during an active ransomware incident. What should it focus on?
options: Business impact, current status and the decisions needed from the board
The full list of indicators of compromise so the board can verify scope
A minute-by-minute log of every analyst action so far
The likely threat actor group, even though attribution is not yet confirmed
quiz.explain: Executives need impact, risk and decisions. IoCs and detailed logs are for technical teams, and unconfirmed attribution should never be presented as fact.

lessons.title: Writing an incident report
lessons.summary: The incident report is the permanent record of what happened and what will change. It is read by executives, auditors, insurers and sometimes lawyers, so it has to be accurate, clear and evidence-based.
points: Typical structure: executive summary, incident details (who, what, when, where, why), timeline, scope and impact, evidence, root cause, recommendations, lessons learned.
Executive summary first, written last: a short, non-technical overview of what happened, the impact, the current status and the decisions or investment needed.
Timeline: normalise every timestamp to one time zone (often UTC) and state it. Cite the source of each entry (firewall, EDR, mailbox audit log).
Scope and impact: systems, accounts and data affected, business disruption, and whether personal information was involved. Label confirmed facts separately from assumptions.
Evidence: what was collected, file hashes and references to chain of custody records, kept separate from the narrative.
Root cause is the underlying control failure (e.g. legacy authentication bypassed MFA), not the trigger (a user clicked a link). Techniques such as the 5 Whys help.
Recommendations are specific and trackable: action, owner, due date and how completion will be verified. Lessons learned are held soon after the incident and stay blameless.
lessons.examTip: If the report is going to non-technical readers, the executive summary is the key section. If the question asks how to stop recurrence, look for root cause and actionable recommendations.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a running timeline in the ticket from the first alert. Rebuilding times from memory a week later is slow and error-prone, and the report will be read by the insurer.

quiz.q: While building an incident timeline, an analyst has firewall logs in UTC, endpoint logs in Australian Eastern Standard Time and cloud audit logs in UTC. What should the analyst do?
options: Normalise all timestamps to one time zone and state it in the report
Keep each source's native timestamps so the evidence is unaltered
Order events by the time the SIEM ingested them
Round all events to the nearest hour to simplify the timeline
quiz.explain: Mixed time zones make the sequence of events wrong. The original logs stay preserved as evidence; the report's timeline uses one stated time zone. Ingestion time is not event time.

quiz.q: A user entered credentials on a phishing page. The attacker then signed in to webmail using a legacy protocol that does not support MFA. What is the best root cause statement?
options: Legacy authentication was left enabled, allowing sign-in without MFA
The user clicked a link in a phishing email
The attacker used a sophisticated phishing kit
The email gateway failed to block the message
quiz.explain: Root cause is the underlying control failure that let the incident happen. Phishing clicks are expected; the missing control (MFA enforced on every sign-in path) is what allowed the compromise.

quiz.q: Which recommendation is best suited for an incident report?
options: Disable legacy authentication for all mailboxes by 30 June; owner: messaging team; verify with sign-in logs
Improve the organisation's overall security awareness
Staff should be more careful with email in future
quiz.explain: Good recommendations are specific, tied to the root cause, and have an owner, a due date and a way to verify completion.
